items.stimulus: The bike lanes the city added to Main Street last year have made the street safer. In the year after the lanes were installed, traffic accidents on Main Street fell by a third.
items.prompt: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

options.text: Most cyclists on Main Street use the new lanes.
options.why: The lanes could improve safety even if many cyclists skip them, for example by slowing cars.

options.text: Bike lanes reduce traffic accidents on every street where they are installed.
options.why: The argument is only about Main Street; it doesn't need a universal claim.

options.text: Accidents on Main Street had been rising before the lanes were installed.
options.why: Even if accidents had been steady, the argument could still work.

options.text: No other change on Main Street during that year accounts for the drop in accidents.
options.why: Negate it and some other change explains the drop, so the lanes get no credit.

options.text: Drivers on Main Street support the bike lanes.
options.why: Drivers' opinions don't bear on whether the lanes caused the drop.

items.tldr: The argument needs nothing else to explain the drop in accidents.

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.body: Accidents fell after the lanes went in, so the argument concludes the lanes caused it.

steps.label: Negation test
steps.body: If another change explains the drop, the causal claim collapses.

items.takeaway: Causal arguments from "after" always assume no other cause did the work.

items.stimulus: Since the Brookfield Library began lending e-books two years ago, checkouts of its print books have fallen by 20 percent. Clearly, many patrons who once borrowed print books from the library now borrow e-books instead.
items.prompt: The argument requires assuming which one of the following?

options.text: Most library patrons prefer e-books to print books.
options.why: The conclusion is about many former print borrowers, not most patrons.

options.text: E-books cost the library less than print books do.
options.why: Cost has nothing to do with why print checkouts fell.

options.text: The library now lends more e-books than print books.
options.why: Some switching can happen without e-books outnumbering print checkouts.

options.text: Patrons who borrow e-books never borrow print books.
options.why: Patrons could borrow both and the argument would still hold.

options.text: The number of people using the library has not declined enough over the past two years to account for the drop in print checkouts.
options.why: If fewer patrons explains the drop, there's no reason to think anyone switched to e-books.

items.tldr: The drop must not just reflect fewer library users.

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.body: Fewer print checkouts, so the argument concludes people switched to e-books.

steps.label: Rival explanation
steps.body: A shrinking number of patrons would also cut print checkouts.

items.takeaway: When a number falls, ask whether the total it comes from fell too.

items.stimulus: Critics claim that the new biology textbook is too difficult for ninth graders. But the textbook was written by a team of experienced high school biology teachers. So the critics are mistaken.
items.prompt: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?

options.text: The critics have never taught ninth-grade biology.
options.why: The argument doesn't depend on anything about the critics' experience.

options.text: No textbook written by experienced teachers has ever been too difficult for its intended students.
options.why: The argument needs teachers to be good judges, not infallible ones.

options.text: Experienced high school biology teachers are generally able to judge what ninth graders can understand.
options.why: If they can't judge that, who wrote the book tells us nothing about its difficulty.

options.text: Ninth graders find biology harder than other subjects.
options.why: That comparison doesn't connect authorship to difficulty.

options.text: The new textbook covers more topics than the one it replaced.
options.why: Coverage isn't the same as difficulty.

items.tldr: The authors' experience counts only if it lets them judge what ninth graders can handle.

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.body: The premise is about who wrote the book; the conclusion is about how hard it is.

steps.label: Bridge
steps.body: Experienced teachers can judge what ninth graders understand.

items.takeaway: An assumption often links the kind of evidence offered to the kind of claim made.

items.stimulus: To reduce littering in Lake Park, the city plans to double the number of trash cans in the park. Because people litter mainly when no trash can is in sight, the plan will reduce littering.
items.prompt: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

options.text: Park visitors know that littering is illegal.
options.why: The argument rests on visible cans, not on knowledge of the law.

options.text: No one litters when a trash can is in sight.
options.why: The premise says people litter mainly when no can is visible; some littering elsewhere is fine.

options.text: Doubling the trash cans will cost less than hiring more cleanup crews.
options.why: Cost compared with another option doesn't affect whether this plan reduces littering.

options.text: Doubling the number of trash cans will put a trash can in sight in some places in the park where none is now visible.
options.why: If the new cans sit only where cans are already visible, the cause of littering is untouched.

options.text: Most of the litter in the park is food packaging.
options.why: The type of litter doesn't affect the plan's logic.

items.tldr: More cans help only if they're visible where cans now aren't.

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.body: Littering happens where no can is in sight; the plan adds cans.

steps.label: Negation test
steps.body: If the new cans don't change where cans are in sight, the plan won't work.

items.takeaway: Plans assume their action actually reaches the cause they target.

items.stimulus: Students at Hillside School scored higher on this year's state reading exam than students at Valley School. So Hillside's reading curriculum is more effective than Valley's.
items.prompt: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

options.text: Every Hillside student outscored every Valley student.
options.why: A higher average is enough for the comparison.

options.text: Valley School plans to adopt Hillside's curriculum.
options.why: Future plans don't bear on which curriculum is more effective.

options.text: Hillside's students did not begin the year with substantially stronger reading skills than Valley's students.
options.why: If Hillside's students started far ahead, the higher scores say nothing about the curriculum.

options.text: The state reading exam is the only valid measure of reading ability.
options.why: The exam needs to be a reasonable measure, not the only one.

options.text: Hillside spends more per student on reading instruction than Valley does.
options.why: Extra spending would be a rival explanation, which hurts the argument.

items.tldr: The groups must have started out comparable.

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.body: Different scores, so the argument concludes the curricula differ in effectiveness.

steps.label: Rival explanation
steps.body: Different students to begin with.

items.takeaway: Comparisons of outcomes assume the groups were comparable at the start.

items.stimulus: In a poll of 1,000 voters reached on landline telephones, 62 percent said they support the library bond measure. So the measure is likely to pass.
items.prompt: The argument depends on the assumption that

options.text: at least 62 percent of eligible voters will cast ballots
options.why: Turnout level doesn't matter if those who vote resemble the sample.

options.text: the mayor supports the bond measure
options.why: The mayor's view isn't part of the argument.

options.text: no voter who was polled will change his or her mind before the election
options.why: A few changed minds wouldn't overturn a 62 percent majority.

options.text: voters reached on landline telephones are not much more likely to support the measure than voters in general
options.why: If landline users favor the measure far more than others, the poll overstates support.

options.text: most voters own landline telephones
options.why: What matters is whether landline users are representative, not how many voters have landlines.

items.tldr: The landline sample must represent voters as a whole.

steps.label: Sample
steps.body: Voters reached on landlines.

steps.label: Negation test
steps.body: If they're much more supportive than other voters, the 62 percent doesn't carry over.

items.takeaway: Arguments from polls assume the sample resembles the population it stands for.

items.stimulus: People who meditate daily report lower levels of stress than people who do not. So daily meditation reduces stress.
items.prompt: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

options.text: People with low levels of stress are not much more likely than others to take up daily meditation.
options.why: If calm people are the ones who take up meditation, the correlation runs the other way.

options.text: People who do not meditate have tried meditating at some point.
options.why: Nonmeditators' past attempts don't affect the causal claim.

options.text: Everyone who meditates daily experiences reduced stress.
options.why: The conclusion is a general tendency, not a claim about everyone.

options.text: Stress can be measured more precisely than by self-report.
options.why: The argument relies on self-reports; it doesn't need better measures to exist.

options.text: Meditation is the most effective way to reduce stress.
options.why: Meditation only has to reduce stress, not beat every alternative.

items.tldr: Low stress must not be what leads people to meditate.

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.body: Meditators are less stressed, so the argument concludes meditation lowers stress.

steps.label: Reverse it
steps.body: If low-stress people simply choose to meditate, the conclusion fails.

items.takeaway: Every causal conclusion from a correlation assumes the cause isn't reversed.

items.stimulus: When the city banned smoking in restaurants, owners predicted they would lose customers, but restaurant revenues rose the following year. Owners now predict that a proposed ban on cell phone use in restaurants will drive customers away. This prediction is likely to prove just as mistaken.
items.prompt: The argument depends on the assumption that

options.text: the smoking ban caused restaurant revenues to rise
options.why: The argument needs only that the ban didn't hurt business, not that it helped.

options.text: the cell phone ban would be strictly enforced
options.why: Enforcement doesn't establish that the two bans are alike in the relevant way.

options.text: most diners use their phones during meals
options.why: How many diners use phones doesn't make the two bans comparable.

options.text: restaurant owners' predictions about their customers are always mistaken
options.why: The argument concerns these two similar predictions, not every prediction.

options.text: diners are not substantially more attached to using their phones during meals than smokers were to smoking during meals
options.why: If diners care much more about phones, the smoking ban is a poor guide to the phone ban.

items.tldr: The two bans must be alike in how much customers care about the banned activity.

steps.label: Structure
steps.body: The smoking ban didn't drive customers away, so the phone ban won't either.

steps.label: Gap
steps.body: The analogy needs the bans to matter to customers about equally.

items.takeaway: Analogies assume no relevant difference between the two cases.

items.stimulus: Kenji wants to join the university's honors program, which admits only students with a grade-point average of at least 3.7. His average is now 3.5, but he plans to raise it to 3.7 by taking three electives next semester. So after next semester Kenji will meet the honors program's grade requirement.
items.prompt: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

options.text: Most students in the honors program have averages above 3.8.
options.why: Other students' averages don't affect whether Kenji reaches 3.7.

options.text: Kenji's electives will be easier than his required courses.
options.why: He needs high enough grades, however hard the courses are.

options.text: A 3.7 average guarantees admission to the honors program.
options.why: The conclusion is only about meeting the grade requirement, not about admission.

options.text: Kenji will not take any courses besides the three electives.
options.why: He could take other courses and still reach 3.7.

options.text: Kenji can earn grades in the three electives high enough to raise his average to 3.7.
options.why: If no achievable grades would lift his average that far, the plan can't succeed.

items.tldr: The plan works only if the electives can actually raise his average enough.

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.body: The plan is to take electives; the conclusion is that his average will reach 3.7.

steps.label: Negation test
steps.body: If no achievable grades get him there, the conclusion fails.

items.takeaway: A plan's success assumes its means can actually produce the result.

items.stimulus: Our new advertising campaign has succeeded in drawing attention to our website: visits to the site rose 40 percent during the six weeks the campaign ran.
items.prompt: The argument requires assuming which one of the following?

options.text: The campaign cost less than previous campaigns.
options.why: Cost doesn't bear on whether the campaign drew attention.

options.text: The rise in visits was not due entirely to factors unrelated to the campaign.
options.why: If something else caused the whole rise, the campaign drew no attention at all.

options.text: Visits will stay 40 percent higher after the campaign ends.
options.why: Lasting effects aren't part of the conclusion.

options.text: Every visitor during the campaign had seen one of the ads.
options.why: The campaign needs to account for some of the rise, not every visit.

options.text: The campaign increased sales as well as visits.
options.why: The conclusion is about attention to the website, not sales.

items.tldr: At least some of the rise must come from the campaign.

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.body: Visits rose during the campaign, so the argument concludes the campaign worked.

steps.label: Negation test
steps.body: If unrelated factors explain the entire rise, the conclusion fails.

items.takeaway: Necessary assumptions are often modest, like "not entirely due to something else."

items.stimulus: A farm cooperative now pays distributors a fee to deliver its produce to city restaurants. It plans to deliver the produce itself, and the restaurants will pay the same prices as before. Because it will no longer pay the distributors' fees, the cooperative expects its members' profits to rise.
items.prompt: The cooperative's expectation depends on which one of the following assumptions?

options.text: Every restaurant that buys from the cooperative will keep doing so for years.
options.why: Profits can rise without every customer staying indefinitely.

options.text: The distributors will lower their fees to keep the cooperative's business.
options.why: Lower fees would make dropping the distributors less attractive, not more.

options.text: City restaurants prefer to buy directly from farms.
options.why: The restaurants have already agreed to keep paying the same prices.

options.text: The cooperative's members currently earn less than the distributors do.
options.why: Comparing incomes doesn't affect whether the plan raises profits.

options.text: The cooperative's own costs of delivering the produce will be lower than the fees it now pays distributors.
options.why: With prices unchanged, profits rise only if doing the deliveries costs less than the fees saved.

items.tldr: The plan pays only if doing the deliveries costs less than the fees saved.

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.body: The fees disappear, but delivering costs something too.

steps.label: Negation test
steps.body: If those costs equal or exceed the fees, profits won't rise.

items.takeaway: Cost-cutting plans assume the replacement costs less than what it replaces.

items.stimulus: After Riverton raised its minimum wage last spring, unemployment among the city's teenagers rose sharply. Evidently, the higher minimum wage caused the rise in teenage unemployment.
items.prompt: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

options.text: Unemployment among adults in Riverton rose as well.
options.why: A general rise would suggest a broader cause, which weakens the argument.

options.text: Every teenager who lost a job had been earning the minimum wage.
options.why: The wage increase could cause the rise without explaining every lost job.

options.text: Other cities that raised their minimum wage saw no rise in teenage unemployment.
options.why: That would count against the causal claim.

options.text: Riverton's increase was larger than increases in nearby cities.
options.why: The size relative to other cities isn't needed for the causal claim.

options.text: Teenage unemployment in Riverton had not already begun rising sharply before the minimum wage increase took effect.
options.why: If the rise started earlier, the wage increase can't be what set it off.

items.tldr: The rise must not have already been under way before the wage increase.

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.body: The argument infers cause from sequence.

steps.label: Negation test
steps.body: If unemployment was already climbing, the sequence proves nothing.

items.takeaway: Arguments from "after X, Y" assume Y wasn't already happening before X.

items.stimulus: Over the past decade, the number of applicants to Hartwell College has grown by about 5 percent every year. So Hartwell should expect more applicants next year than it received this year.
items.prompt: The argument depends on the assumption that

options.text: most of Hartwell's applicants live out of state
options.why: Where applicants live doesn't affect whether the trend continues.

options.text: no development is likely to reverse the trend in Hartwell's applications next year
options.why: If something likely will reverse the trend, the past decade is no basis for the expectation.

options.text: Hartwell will admit more students next year than it did this year
options.why: Admissions don't determine how many people apply.

options.text: Hartwell's applications will grow by exactly 5 percent next year
options.why: Any growth satisfies the conclusion.

options.text: applications to other colleges are declining
options.why: Other colleges' trends don't bear on Hartwell's.

items.tldr: Projecting a trend assumes nothing is likely to break it.

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.body: Past growth, so the argument expects more growth.

steps.label: Negation test
steps.body: If a reversal is likely, the expectation is unjustified.

items.takeaway: Predictions from trends assume the conditions behind the trend continue.

items.stimulus: Region X reported more cases of influenza this winter than Region Y did. So influenza was more widespread in Region X than in Region Y this winter.
items.prompt: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

options.text: Region Y reported fewer cases this winter than it did last winter.
options.why: Region Y's own trend doesn't bear on the comparison.

options.text: Influenza will also be more widespread in Region X next winter.
options.why: The conclusion concerns this winter only.

options.text: Region X has more hospitals than Region Y.
options.why: Hospital counts don't establish how widespread the flu was.

options.text: Region X's larger number of cases is not explained by its having a much larger population than Region Y.
options.why: If Region X is simply much bigger, more cases don't mean a higher rate.

options.text: Every case of influenza in both regions was reported.
options.why: Reporting needs to be comparable, not complete.

items.tldr: More cases mean wider spread only if the populations are comparable.

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.body: Raw case counts, so the argument concludes the flu was more widespread.

steps.label: Negation test
steps.body: If the gap reflects population size, the conclusion fails.

items.takeaway: "More cases" supports "more widespread" only with comparable populations.

items.stimulus: The ancient building had no windows and a single narrow entrance, and archaeologists found large quantities of grain residue on its floor. It must originally have been built as a granary.
items.prompt: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

options.text: All ancient granaries lacked windows.
options.why: The argument needs windowless buildings to suit grain storage, not every granary to be windowless.

options.text: The grain residue was not left by a later use of the building, long after its original purpose had ended.
options.why: If the residue came from later occupants, it says nothing about why the building was built.

options.text: The building was the largest in the settlement.
options.why: Its size isn't part of the reasoning.

options.text: Grain was the settlement's most important food.
options.why: Grain needn't be the main food for the building to be a granary.

options.text: No other building in the settlement had a single entrance.
options.why: Other buildings could share the feature without undermining the conclusion.

items.tldr: The residue must date from the building's original use.

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.body: The conclusion is about the original purpose; the residue could date from any time.

steps.label: Negation test
steps.body: Residue left by later users wouldn't support the conclusion.

items.takeaway: Watch for time gaps between when evidence was produced and what the conclusion is about.

items.stimulus: The average sale price of houses in Linwood rose by 15 percent last year. So people who owned homes in Linwood at the start of last year saw their homes increase in value.
items.prompt: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

options.text: Linwood's homeowners intend to sell their houses.
options.why: A home can rise in value whether or not it's sold.

options.text: House prices in neighboring towns rose as well.
options.why: Neighboring towns don't affect Linwood's homeowners.

options.text: Every house in Linwood rose in value by 15 percent.
options.why: The conclusion says homes increased in value, not by a uniform 15 percent.

options.text: More houses were sold in Linwood last year than the year before.
options.why: The number of sales doesn't show whether values rose.

options.text: The rise in the average sale price was not due entirely to a change in the kinds of houses that were sold.
options.why: If the average rose only because pricier houses happened to sell, existing homes may not have gained value.

items.tldr: A rising average can reflect which houses sold, not rising values.

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.body: The average sale price is about houses sold; the conclusion is about houses owned.

steps.label: Negation test
steps.body: If the mix of sales explains the rise, owners' values may not have changed.

items.takeaway: Averages can shift because the group changed, not because its members did.

items.stimulus: Of the restaurants that have been open in Fairview for more than twenty years, nearly all serve traditional local dishes. Clearly, serving traditional local dishes helps a restaurant survive in Fairview.
items.prompt: The argument depends on the assumption that

options.text: Fairview's residents prefer traditional local dishes to other food
options.why: This might explain the pattern, but the argument doesn't require it.

options.text: traditional local dishes are cheaper to prepare than other dishes
options.why: The argument needn't identify how the dishes help.

options.text: it is not the case that nearly all restaurants that have opened in Fairview, including those that later closed, served traditional local dishes
options.why: If nearly every restaurant served them, the survivors would too, and the dishes would explain nothing.

options.text: restaurants that serve traditional local dishes never close
options.why: The dishes only need to help survival, not guarantee it.

options.text: most of Fairview's restaurants are more than twenty years old
options.why: How many restaurants are old doesn't matter to the comparison.

items.tldr: Survivors' menus mean something only if failed restaurants' menus differed.

steps.label: Sample
steps.body: Only surviving restaurants were examined.

steps.label: Negation test
steps.body: If nearly all restaurants, including the failures, served these dishes, the pattern says nothing about survival.

items.takeaway: Survivorship arguments assume the failures differed from the survivors.

items.stimulus: Patients who took part in the hospital's new physical therapy program recovered from knee surgery faster than patients who did not. So the program speeds recovery from knee surgery.
items.prompt: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

options.text: Patients were not chosen for the program because they were already recovering faster than others.
options.why: If faster recoverers were picked for the program, their speed reflects selection, not the program.

options.text: Knee surgery patients usually take several months to recover.
options.why: The typical recovery time doesn't affect the comparison.

options.text: The program is the most effective therapy available.
options.why: The program needs to help, not to be the best.

options.text: The program costs less than other therapy programs.
options.why: Cost has nothing to do with whether it speeds recovery.

options.text: All patients in the program recover faster than all patients outside it.
options.why: A faster recovery on average is enough.

items.tldr: The program's patients must not have been picked for their fast recovery.

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.body: Program patients recovered faster, so the argument credits the program.

steps.label: Rival explanation
steps.body: Selection of the fastest recoverers would produce the same result.

items.takeaway: Without random assignment, assume the groups weren't selected in a way that explains the result.

items.stimulus: Installing solar panels on the town hall would reduce the town's electricity bills. Therefore, the town should install solar panels on the town hall.
items.prompt: The argument depends on the assumption that

options.text: most residents favor solar power
options.why: Public opinion isn't part of the argument.

options.text: the town hall uses more electricity than any other town building
options.why: The recommendation concerns the town hall, whatever other buildings use.

options.text: solar panels last at least fifty years
options.why: They need to last long enough to pay off, not fifty years.

options.text: the savings from the panels would not be outweighed by the costs of buying and installing them
options.why: If the panels cost more than they save, lower bills alone don't justify installing them.

options.text: electricity prices will rise in the coming years
options.why: Rising prices would add to the savings, but the argument doesn't need them.

items.tldr: "Should" requires that benefits outweigh costs.

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.body: One benefit (lower bills), so the argument concludes the town should act.

steps.label: Negation test
steps.body: If costs outweigh savings, the recommendation fails.

items.takeaway: Recommendations based on a benefit assume no greater cost.

items.stimulus: People who drink green tea daily have lower blood levels of protein C-7, a protein released during inflammation, than people who don't. So drinking green tea daily reduces inflammation.
items.prompt: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

options.text: Lower blood levels of protein C-7 indicate lower levels of inflammation.
options.why: If C-7 levels don't track inflammation, lower C-7 says nothing about inflammation.

options.text: Protein C-7 is found only in human blood.
options.why: Where else the protein occurs doesn't matter here.

options.text: Green tea is the only beverage that lowers levels of protein C-7.
options.why: Other drinks could lower C-7 without affecting the argument.

options.text: People who drink green tea daily also exercise more than others.
options.why: Exercise would be a rival explanation, which hurts the argument.

options.text: Inflammation is the main cause of most chronic diseases.
options.why: The argument doesn't concern disease.

items.tldr: The argument treats C-7 as a marker for inflammation.

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.body: The evidence is about C-7; the conclusion is about inflammation.

steps.label: Bridge
steps.body: C-7 levels must actually reflect inflammation.

items.takeaway: When evidence measures a marker, the argument assumes the marker tracks the real thing.

items.stimulus: To cut its paper costs, the Kessling office will require employees to print documents double-sided. Since double-sided printing uses half as many sheets per document, the office's paper costs will fall.
items.prompt: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

options.text: Paper is the office's largest expense.
options.why: The argument concerns paper costs only.

options.text: The requirement will not lead employees to print so many more documents that total paper use stays the same or rises.
options.why: If employees print twice as much, fewer sheets per document won't cut costs.

options.text: Every document the office prints is more than one page long.
options.why: Savings on multipage documents are enough, even if some documents are one page.

options.text: Double-sided printing is faster than single-sided printing.
options.why: Speed doesn't affect paper costs.

options.text: Employees prefer reading double-sided documents.
options.why: Preferences don't determine paper use under a requirement.

items.tldr: Fewer sheets per document saves money only if the number of documents doesn't balloon.

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.body: The premise is about sheets per document; the conclusion is about total cost.

steps.label: Negation test
steps.body: Enough extra printing would wipe out the savings.

items.takeaway: Per-unit savings assume the number of units doesn't rise enough to cancel them.

items.stimulus: When the Oak Street Bakery began posting its daily specials online, its sales rose. So the other bakeries in town would also increase their sales by posting their daily specials online.
items.prompt: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

options.text: Posting specials online costs bakeries very little.
options.why: Cost doesn't affect whether sales rise.

options.text: Every bakery in town offers daily specials.
options.why: The conclusion concerns bakeries posting their specials; it doesn't need all of them to have specials.

options.text: The customers of the other bakeries in town are not much less likely than Oak Street's customers to look for daily specials online.
options.why: If other bakeries' customers rarely look online, posting specials won't help those bakeries.

options.text: Oak Street's sales rose only because of its online specials.
options.why: The specials need to have helped, not to be the only cause.

options.text: The Oak Street Bakery's sales rose more than any other bakery's.
options.why: Ranking the bakeries doesn't connect Oak Street's case to the others.

items.tldr: Other bakeries must resemble Oak Street in the way that made posting work.

steps.label: Structure
steps.body: It worked at one bakery, so it would work at others.

steps.label: Gap
steps.body: The other bakeries' customers must be comparably reachable online.

items.takeaway: Generalizing from one case assumes the other cases are relevantly similar.

items.stimulus: Most employees at Calloway Inc. work more than fifty hours a week. So Calloway is not a company that values its employees' well-being.
items.prompt: The argument depends on the assumption that

options.text: most of Calloway's competitors require fewer hours
options.why: Competitors' policies don't bear on what Calloway values.

options.text: Calloway's employees are paid less than those at similar companies
options.why: Pay isn't part of the argument.

options.text: employees who work more than fifty hours a week are less productive
options.why: Productivity isn't the issue; well-being is.

options.text: no company whose employees work long hours values their well-being
options.why: This would guarantee the conclusion, but the argument needs less.

options.text: Calloway does not let its employees work fewer hours without penalty
options.why: If employees could cut back freely and simply chose long hours, their schedules wouldn't show what Calloway values.

items.tldr: Long hours reflect the company's values only if employees can't freely choose shorter ones.

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.body: The evidence is about hours worked; the conclusion is about what the company values.

steps.label: Defend against an objection
steps.body: The argument must rule out that the long hours are freely chosen.

items.takeaway: Necessary assumptions often rule out one specific objection, not every possible one.

items.stimulus: Of the drivers stopped at a sobriety checkpoint on Route 9 last weekend, fewer than one percent were driving under the influence of alcohol. So drunk driving is not a serious problem in the county.
items.prompt: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

options.text: Fewer people drive at night on weekends than on weekdays.
options.why: Driving patterns by day don't bear on the checkpoint's sample.

options.text: The checkpoint stopped every driver who used Route 9 last weekend.
options.why: A fair sample of drivers is enough.

options.text: Drivers who had been drinking did not avoid Route 9 last weekend in disproportionate numbers.
options.why: If drinking drivers steered clear of the checkpoint, the one percent figure understates the problem.

options.text: Penalties for drunk driving in the county are severe.
options.why: Penalties don't establish how common drunk driving is.

options.text: Drunk driving causes most traffic accidents in the county.
options.why: That would suggest drunk driving is a serious problem, the opposite of the conclusion.

items.tldr: The checkpoint sample is useful only if drinking drivers didn't dodge it.

steps.label: Sample
steps.body: Drivers stopped at one checkpoint on one weekend.

steps.label: Negation test
steps.body: If drinking drivers avoided the route, the sample is skewed toward sober drivers.

items.takeaway: Samples that people can choose to avoid tend to undercount what they're avoiding.

items.stimulus: Dr. Ruiz, who has studied the region's wildlife for thirty years, says that the region's gray wolf population is growing. So the gray wolf population in the region is growing.
items.prompt: The argument depends on the assumption that

options.text: Dr. Ruiz has published more studies than any other researcher in the region
options.why: Her rank among researchers doesn't establish reliability about wolves.

options.text: gray wolves are the most studied animal in the region
options.why: How much others study wolves doesn't matter.

options.text: Dr. Ruiz's long study of the region's wildlife gives her reliable knowledge of its gray wolf population
options.why: If her experience doesn't extend reliably to wolves, her say-so isn't good evidence.

options.text: experts on wildlife are never wrong about population trends
options.why: The argument needs her to be reliable, not infallible.

options.text: the gray wolf population will continue to grow for many years
options.why: The conclusion concerns the current trend only.

items.tldr: An expert's claim is evidence only if her expertise reliably covers the claim.

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.body: The argument rests entirely on her testimony.

steps.label: Negation test
steps.body: If her knowledge of wolves isn't reliable, the testimony gives no support.

items.takeaway: Appeals to authority assume the authority's expertise covers this particular claim.

items.stimulus: The museum describes its new exhibit as a "free" experience, meaning visitors may explore its rooms in any order they choose. Yet the museum charges admission to the exhibit. So the museum's description is false.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: treats a word used in one sense in the museum's description as if it were used in a different sense
options.why: The museum meant "free to explore in any order"; the argument reads it as "no charge."

options.text: concludes that a claim is false merely because it has not been proven true
options.why: The argument offers a reason (the admission charge), not a lack of proof.

options.text: assumes that what is true of the exhibit is true of the museum as a whole
options.why: The argument makes no claim about the museum as a whole.

options.text: relies on the testimony of museum staff who may have a motive to mislead
options.why: No testimony is cited.

options.text: fails to consider that admission prices may change in the future
options.why: Future prices don't bear on whether the description was false.

items.tldr: "Free" meant free to wander, not free of charge, so the charge doesn't make the description false.

steps.label: Spot the word
steps.body: The whole argument turns on "free."

steps.label: Compare senses
steps.body: The museum's sense is about movement; the critic's sense is about price.

items.takeaway: When an argument turns on a single word, check whether it keeps the same meaning throughout.

items.stimulus: Columnist: Greenfield's mayor is the most trustworthy official in the region. After all, she has never told the public anything false, and we can be confident of that because a trustworthy official like her would never mislead the public.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the columnist's argument is flawed because it

options.text: attacks the character of the mayor's critics rather than their arguments
options.why: No critics are mentioned.

options.text: takes for granted that the mayor's popularity proves her trustworthiness
options.why: Popularity never comes up.

options.text: confuses a necessary condition for trustworthiness with a sufficient one
options.why: The problem is circularity, not a conditional reversal.

options.text: draws a conclusion about all officials from the case of a single official
options.why: The conclusion is about the mayor alone.

options.text: presupposes the truth of its conclusion in offering support for one of its premises
options.why: Her honesty is "shown" by assuming she's trustworthy, which is the conclusion itself.

items.tldr: It proves she's trustworthy by assuming she's trustworthy. That's circular.

steps.label: Trace support
steps.body: Conclusion ← she never lied ← a trustworthy official wouldn't lie.

steps.label: Notice
steps.body: The last link assumes the conclusion, so nothing independent supports it.

items.takeaway: If a premise only makes sense once you accept the conclusion, the argument is circular.

items.stimulus: Either the city raises property taxes or it closes two of its public libraries. Since raising property taxes would hurt the city's homeowners, the city should close the libraries.
items.prompt: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

options.text: treats a claim about the city's budget as if it were a claim about its residents
options.why: The argument doesn't blur those claims.

options.text: assumes that whatever hurts homeowners also hurts renters
options.why: Renters are never mentioned.

options.text: fails to consider that there may be options other than raising property taxes or closing libraries
options.why: The city might cut other spending, find grants or raise other fees.

options.text: relies on an appeal to popular opinion
options.why: No one's opinion is cited.

options.text: draws a general conclusion from a single example
options.why: No example is used.

items.tldr: It assumes those are the only two choices.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: Tax or close libraries; tax hurts homeowners; so close libraries.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: The "either/or" premise ignores every other way to balance the budget.

items.takeaway: "Either X or Y" premises are suspect: ask whether there's a third option.

items.stimulus: Dr. Lim, a renowned cardiologist, says that the new tax on sugary drinks will have no effect on the local economy. So the tax will have no effect on the local economy.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: confuses what will happen with what should happen
options.why: Both claims are about what will happen.

options.text: attacks Dr. Lim's motives instead of evaluating her claim
options.why: The argument accepts her claim; it doesn't attack her.

options.text: relies on the opinion of an expert on a matter outside her area of expertise
options.why: A cardiologist's training doesn't make her an authority on economics.

options.text: assumes that a tax that affects health will also affect the economy
options.why: The argument concludes there will be no economic effect.

options.text: treats a correlation as evidence of causation
options.why: No correlation is cited.

items.tldr: A heart specialist's view on economics isn't expert evidence.

steps.label: Source
steps.body: The only support is Dr. Lim's say-so.

steps.label: Fit
steps.body: Her expertise (cardiology) doesn't cover the claim (economic effects).

items.takeaway: Expert testimony counts only within the expert's field.

items.stimulus: A recent poll found that 70 percent of residents believe the proposed highway will reduce traffic downtown. Since so many residents agree, the highway will reduce downtown traffic.
items.prompt: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

options.text: assumes that reducing traffic is the highway's only purpose
options.why: The argument doesn't discuss the highway's purposes.

options.text: fails to consider that the highway's costs may outweigh its benefits
options.why: The conclusion is about traffic, not whether the highway is worth it.

options.text: treats the fact that many people believe a claim as sufficient evidence that it is true
options.why: Widespread belief about traffic isn't evidence about traffic.

options.text: relies on a poll of residents who do not live downtown
options.why: The stimulus doesn't say where the respondents live.

options.text: confuses a cause with an effect
options.why: No causal reversal occurs.

items.tldr: Seventy percent believing it doesn't make it true.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: The only support is what most residents believe.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: Belief, however common, isn't evidence that the belief is correct.

items.takeaway: Popularity is evidence of opinion, not of fact.

items.stimulus: Councilor Diaz has proposed lowering the speed limit on Elm Street from 35 to 25 miles per hour. But banning cars from Elm Street entirely would devastate the businesses there. Diaz's proposal should therefore be rejected.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: concludes that a proposal will fail merely because it has not been tried
options.why: Novelty isn't the stated reason.

options.text: argues against a position more extreme than the one actually proposed
options.why: Diaz proposed a lower speed limit, not a ban on cars.

options.text: assumes that what benefits businesses also benefits residents
options.why: Residents' interests never come up.

options.text: attacks Diaz's character rather than her proposal
options.why: It attacks a (distorted) proposal, not Diaz herself.

options.text: relies on a sample that is unrepresentative
options.why: No sample is involved.

items.tldr: It refutes a car ban nobody proposed. That's a straw man.

steps.label: Proposal
steps.body: Lower the limit from 35 to 25.

steps.label: Argument
steps.body: Rebuts a total ban, a much stronger position, then rejects the real proposal.

items.takeaway: Check whether the view being attacked is the view actually held.

items.stimulus: Last month I ate at two restaurants in Port Ellis, and both served undercooked fish. Clearly, the restaurants in Port Ellis do not follow food-safety standards.
items.prompt: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

options.text: relies on a source with a stake in the outcome
options.why: No interested source is involved.

options.text: draws a broad conclusion about a group on the basis of too few cases
options.why: Two meals can't show what all of the town's restaurants do.

options.text: mistakes a lack of evidence for evidence that something is false
options.why: The argument cites positive evidence, just too little of it.

options.text: confuses a necessary condition with a sufficient one
options.why: No conditional reasoning appears.

options.text: presumes that what is true of a group is true of each of its members
options.why: The argument runs from members to the group, not the reverse.

items.tldr: Two restaurants can't speak for every restaurant in town.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Two bad meals at two restaurants.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: A claim about all the town's restaurants, which is far broader than the evidence.

items.takeaway: Watch the gap between how many cases are cited and how broad the conclusion is.

items.stimulus: No study has ever shown that the herbal supplement Calmera improves sleep. Therefore, Calmera does not improve sleep.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: confuses improving sleep with curing insomnia
options.why: Insomnia isn't mentioned.

options.text: takes the lack of evidence for a claim as proof that the claim is false
options.why: No study showing an effect isn't the same as studies showing no effect.

options.text: relies on studies funded by the supplement's manufacturer
options.why: No studies are cited at all.

options.text: generalizes from a small number of studies
options.why: The point is that there are no supporting studies.

options.text: assumes that what helps some people sleep helps everyone sleep
options.why: The argument makes no claim about who is helped.

items.tldr: "Not shown to work" doesn't mean "shown not to work."

steps.label: Premise
steps.body: No evidence that it works.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: It doesn't work, which needs evidence against it, not just missing evidence for it.

items.takeaway: Absence of proof is not proof of absence.

items.stimulus: The proposed factory could release pollutants into the Redwater River. Pollution in the river would harm the fish that local anglers depend on. So if the factory is built, the anglers' catch will decline.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: treats something that could happen as if it will happen
options.why: The factory "could" pollute, but the conclusion says the catch "will" decline.

options.text: confuses a cause of pollution with an effect of pollution
options.why: The causal chain runs in a sensible direction.

options.text: fails to weigh the factory's economic benefits
options.why: The conclusion is about the catch, not overall worth.

options.text: concludes that a factory is harmful merely because it is new
options.why: The argument gives a reason beyond newness.

options.text: relies on the testimony of anglers who oppose the factory
options.why: No anglers are quoted.

items.tldr: "Could pollute" becomes "will reduce the catch." A possibility is treated as certain.

steps.label: Find the hedge
steps.body: "Could release pollutants."

steps.label: Find the jump
steps.body: "Will decline" assumes the pollution actually happens.

items.takeaway: Watch for "may" or "could" in the premises and "will" in the conclusion.

items.stimulus: Shortly after the town of Millbrook painted its fire hydrants bright yellow, the number of house fires in Millbrook declined. Evidently, the yellow paint helped prevent house fires.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: infers that one event caused another merely because the second followed the first
options.why: Fires declining after the painting doesn't show the painting caused the decline.

options.text: assumes that yellow is the only color that would have helped
options.why: The argument never compares colors.

options.text: presumes that hydrants are used to fight every house fire
options.why: That presumption isn't needed for the argument as stated.

options.text: attacks the motives of those who opposed painting the hydrants
options.why: No opponents appear.

options.text: confuses the number of fires with the damage they cause
options.why: Damage isn't discussed.

items.tldr: Before-and-after timing alone doesn't show the paint did anything.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Paint, then fewer fires.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: Sequence isn't cause. Weather, inspections or chance could explain the drop.

items.takeaway: "After this, therefore because of this" is a flaw. Look for a rival explanation.

items.stimulus: To cut its carbon emissions by 20 percent, the Halcyon Corporation must stop operating its oldest factory, since that factory produces 20 percent of the company's emissions.
items.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the argument?

options.text: It relies on emissions figures supplied by the company itself.
options.why: The source of the figures isn't mentioned.

options.text: It concludes that the company will close the factory merely because it should.
options.why: The argument says the company must close it, not that it will.

options.text: It assumes that the oldest factory is also the least profitable.
options.why: Profit never comes up.

options.text: It treats a reduction in emissions as a reduction in every kind of pollution.
options.why: Only emissions are discussed.

options.text: It overlooks the possibility that the company could cut emissions by the same amount in other ways.
options.why: Closing that factory is one way to hit 20 percent, not the only one.

items.tldr: Closing that factory is one way to cut 20 percent, not the only way.

steps.label: Claim
steps.body: "Must" close the factory to reach the goal.

steps.label: Gap
steps.body: Efficiency upgrades or cuts elsewhere could reach the same 20 percent.

items.takeaway: "Must" claims about reaching a goal often ignore other routes to it.

items.stimulus: To be admitted to the Bellmont Conservatory, an applicant must pass a rigorous audition. Theo passed the audition, so he will be admitted to the conservatory.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: draws a conclusion about all applicants from one applicant's case
options.why: The conclusion is about Theo only.

options.text: relies on Theo's own report that he passed
options.why: The stimulus states that he passed.

options.text: presumes that the audition is the conservatory's only requirement for graduation
options.why: Graduation isn't the issue; the argument is about admission.

options.text: treats a requirement for admission as if it guaranteed admission
options.why: Passing is necessary, but other requirements could still keep Theo out.

options.text: assumes that every applicant who fails the audition will reapply
options.why: Reapplying isn't discussed.

items.tldr: "Must pass to get in" doesn't mean "passing gets you in."

steps.label: Map
steps.body: Admitted → passed audition. Theo passed, so the argument concludes Theo is admitted.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: That reverses the conditional, treating a requirement as a guarantee.

items.takeaway: "Must" introduces a necessary condition. Meeting it isn't enough.

items.stimulus: The Westfield Symphony won this year's statewide orchestra competition. So each of its musicians must be among the best musicians in the state.
items.prompt: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

options.text: confuses the orchestra's past success with its future success
options.why: No prediction is made.

options.text: treats a competition result as if it were a matter of opinion
options.why: The argument takes the result as fact.

options.text: assumes that a property of a whole group must belong to each of its members
options.why: An orchestra can win as an ensemble even if some individual players aren't top-tier.

options.text: assumes that a property of each member must belong to the whole group
options.why: That's the opposite direction. This argument runs from the group to each member.

options.text: generalizes from a single performance to the orchestra's entire history
options.why: The conclusion is about the musicians, not the orchestra's history.

items.tldr: The best orchestra needn't consist entirely of the best musicians.

steps.label: Direction
steps.body: Whole (the orchestra won) to parts (each musician is the best).

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: That's division. Group success can come from teamwork or a few stars.

items.takeaway: What's true of a group isn't automatically true of each member.

items.stimulus: This year, 40 percent of the cars sold at Avalon Motors were electric, up from 25 percent last year. So Avalon Motors sold more electric cars this year than last year.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: assumes that electric cars are more profitable than other cars
options.why: Profit isn't mentioned.

options.text: presumes that the customers who bought electric cars were satisfied
options.why: Satisfaction isn't part of the argument.

options.text: relies on sales figures from only two years
options.why: Comparing two years is fine. The issue is shares versus counts.

options.text: confuses the popularity of electric cars with their quality
options.why: Quality isn't discussed.

options.text: overlooks the possibility that Avalon sold far fewer cars in total this year
options.why: 40 percent of a small total can be fewer cars than 25 percent of a large one.

items.tldr: A bigger share of fewer total sales can mean fewer electric cars.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Electric cars' share rose from 25% to 40%.

steps.label: Gap
steps.body: The conclusion is about a count, which depends on total sales too.

items.takeaway: Percentages alone can't establish amounts. Ask what happened to the total.

items.stimulus: To find out whether residents of Clearwater support building a new public pool, the city surveyed people leaving its existing community swim center. Ninety percent supported the new pool. Clearly, most Clearwater residents support it.
items.prompt: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

options.text: assumes that residents who support the pool would use it
options.why: Use isn't part of the conclusion.

options.text: relies on a survey too small to be reliable
options.why: The survey's size isn't given; the problem is who was asked.

options.text: draws a conclusion about all residents from a group likely to be more favorable than residents in general
options.why: People at a swim center are likelier than average to want a pool.

options.text: treats a claim about the pool's popularity as a claim about its value
options.why: The conclusion is only about support.

options.text: fails to consider the cost of building the pool
options.why: The conclusion is about support, not cost.

items.tldr: Swimmers aren't a fair sample of residents on a pool question.

steps.label: Sample
steps.body: People leaving a swim center.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: They differ from residents in exactly the way that affects the answer.

items.takeaway: A biased sample can't support a conclusion about the whole population.

items.stimulus: Professor Okafor's study concludes that the city's new bus routes have shortened commute times. But Professor Okafor rides the bus to work every day, so her conclusion cannot be trusted.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: confuses a correlation with a cause
options.why: No correlation is cited.

options.text: presumes that people who ride the bus prefer shorter commutes
options.why: Preferences aren't part of the argument.

options.text: assumes that commute time is the only measure of a bus system's success
options.why: The argument doesn't discuss measures of success.

options.text: dismisses a conclusion because of a fact about the person who reached it rather than the evidence for it
options.why: Riding the bus doesn't show her study's evidence is bad.

options.text: relies on a single study
options.why: The argument rejects the study rather than relying on it.

items.tldr: It attacks the researcher, not her research.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: Conclusion: distrust the study. Reason: the author rides the bus.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: A personal connection can suggest checking the work, but it doesn't refute it.

items.takeaway: Rejecting a claim because of who made it is an ad hominem flaw.

items.stimulus: Children who eat breakfast every day earn higher grades than children who skip breakfast. So eating breakfast every day improves children's grades.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

options.text: presumes that what is true of children is true of adults
options.why: Adults aren't mentioned.

options.text: treats a claim about most children as a claim about every child
options.why: The comparison is between groups; no "every child" claim is made.

options.text: overlooks the possibility that some other factor, such as a structured home routine, leads both to daily breakfasts and to higher grades
options.why: A third factor could explain both, so the correlation doesn't show breakfast causes better grades.

options.text: assumes that all breakfasts are equally nutritious
options.why: The argument doesn't need that assumption.

options.text: relies on grades as the only measure of learning
options.why: The conclusion is about grades specifically.

items.tldr: A shared cause, like a stable home routine, could produce both breakfasts and grades.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Breakfast eaters get better grades.

steps.label: Gap
steps.body: Correlation treated as cause. A common factor could produce both.

items.takeaway: Before accepting "X causes Y," look for a third factor that causes both.

items.stimulus: People who own dogs report being happier than people who do not. So owning a dog makes people happier.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: confuses owning a dog with caring for a dog
options.why: That distinction plays no role.

options.text: ignores the possibility that happier people are more likely to choose to own dogs
options.why: The causation could run the other way.

options.text: assumes that dog owners own only one dog
options.why: The number of dogs doesn't matter here.

options.text: relies on self-reports that are known to be false
options.why: Nothing says the reports are false.

options.text: generalizes from dogs to all pets
options.why: The conclusion is only about dogs.

items.tldr: Maybe happiness leads to dog ownership, not the other way around.

steps.label: Claim
steps.body: Dogs → happiness.

steps.label: Alternative
steps.body: Happiness → choosing a dog explains the same correlation.

items.takeaway: For any "X causes Y" from a correlation, consider whether Y causes X.

items.stimulus: Critic: The science museum describes natural selection as a theory. But a theory is just a guess. So the museum admits that natural selection is only a guess.
items.prompt: The critic's reasoning is flawed because it

options.text: relies on a shift between a scientific and an everyday meaning of a key word
options.why: A scientific theory is a well-tested explanation; the everyday "theory" is a hunch.

options.text: treats the museum's description as the only evidence for natural selection
options.why: The argument says nothing about other evidence.

options.text: assumes that scientific claims can never be revised
options.why: Revision isn't discussed.

options.text: generalizes from one museum to all museums
options.why: The conclusion is about this museum's description.

options.text: rejects a claim because of who made it
options.why: The museum's credibility isn't attacked.

items.tldr: "Theory" means a tested explanation in science, not a guess.

steps.label: Key word
steps.body: "Theory."

steps.label: Two senses
steps.body: The museum uses the scientific sense; the critic substitutes the everyday sense.

items.takeaway: Equivocation hides in words with both technical and everyday meanings.

items.stimulus: The Riverside Review publishes only the finest poetry, because every poem it prints meets the highest standards. And we know the poems meet those standards because they appear in the Riverside Review.
items.prompt: The argument's reasoning is flawed because it

options.text: relies on the opinion of the journal's own editors
options.why: No editor is quoted.

options.text: confuses the quantity of poems with their quality
options.why: Quantity isn't discussed.

options.text: uses its conclusion as support for one of the claims offered in support of that conclusion
options.why: Appearing in the Review is used to prove quality, which is used to prove the Review's standards.

options.text: overlooks the possibility that other journals also publish fine poetry
options.why: The claim is about what the Review publishes, not about other journals.

options.text: assumes that popular poems are of high quality
options.why: Popularity isn't mentioned.

items.tldr: Good because it's in the Review; in the Review because it's good. That's a circle.

steps.label: Trace
steps.body: Finest poetry ← meets standards ← appears in the Review.

steps.label: Notice
steps.body: Appearing in the Review is exactly what's in question.

items.takeaway: Circular arguments return to their starting point without outside support.

items.stimulus: Ana: Either you support the new stadium or you don't care about our city's economy. You've said you oppose the stadium, so clearly you don't care about the economy.
items.prompt: The reasoning in Ana's argument is flawed because it

options.text: confuses the stadium's cost with its benefits
options.why: Costs and benefits aren't discussed.

options.text: generalizes from one city to all cities
options.why: Only one city is involved.

options.text: assumes that the stadium will be built
options.why: The argument doesn't predict whether it will be built.

options.text: relies on an authority on economics
options.why: No authority is cited.

options.text: presents two alternatives as the only possibilities when others exist
options.why: Someone can care about the economy and still oppose this stadium.

items.tldr: Opposing the stadium and caring about the economy are compatible.

steps.label: Premise
steps.body: Support it, or you don't care about the economy.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: That ignores people who care about the economy but think the stadium is a bad deal.

items.takeaway: Test "either/or" claims by looking for someone who fits neither box.

items.stimulus: The famous actor Jonah Price uses Brightsmile toothpaste and says it is the best on the market. So Brightsmile must be the best toothpaste available.
items.prompt: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

options.text: draws a conclusion about all toothpastes from one brand
options.why: The conclusion is about Brightsmile.

options.text: attacks the motives of a competing toothpaste maker
options.why: No competitor is mentioned.

options.text: confuses a product's price with its quality
options.why: Price isn't mentioned.

options.text: treats the endorsement of someone with no relevant expertise as proof of a claim
options.why: Being a famous actor doesn't make Price an expert on toothpaste.

options.text: assumes that the best toothpaste is also the most popular
options.why: Popularity isn't the argument's evidence.

items.tldr: A celebrity endorsement isn't expert evidence.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: An actor's personal preference.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: He has no expertise that would make his opinion strong evidence.

items.takeaway: Endorsements from non-experts are testimony, not proof.

items.stimulus: My grandfather smoked a pack of cigarettes a day and lived to be ninety-five. So smoking cannot be as harmful to health as doctors claim.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: appeals to the authority of doctors
options.why: The argument rejects the doctors' claim.

options.text: generalizes from all smokers to a single smoker
options.why: It runs the other way: one case is used against a general claim.

options.text: presumes that doctors have a financial motive to exaggerate
options.why: No motive is suggested.

options.text: treats a possible harm as if it were a certain harm
options.why: The argument does the reverse, discounting a likely harm.

options.text: relies on a single case to reject a claim about general tendencies
options.why: Doctors' claim is about risk across many people; one long-lived smoker doesn't refute it.

items.tldr: One exception doesn't disprove a general health risk.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: One smoker who lived long.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: General claims about risk survive individual exceptions.

items.takeaway: Anecdotes can't overturn claims about general tendencies.

items.stimulus: No one has ever shown that the old Harlow mansion is not haunted. So the mansion must be haunted.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: treats the failure to disprove a claim as proof that the claim is true
options.why: That nobody has disproved it isn't evidence that it's true.

options.text: attacks the credibility of skeptics
options.why: No skeptics are mentioned.

options.text: confuses a cause with its effect
options.why: No causal claim is made.

options.text: relies on the testimony of people who say they have seen ghosts
options.why: No testimony is cited.

options.text: assumes that what is true of one mansion is true of all old buildings
options.why: The conclusion concerns only this mansion.

items.tldr: "Not disproved" isn't "proved."

steps.label: Premise
steps.body: No evidence against the claim.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: The conclusion needs evidence for it.

items.takeaway: Lack of disproof, like lack of proof, settles nothing by itself.

items.stimulus: Most first-time novelists do not earn back their publisher's advance. Dana is a first-time novelist. So Dana will not earn back her advance.
items.prompt: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

options.text: treats what is true of most members of a group as certain to be true of a particular member
options.why: "Most" leaves room for Dana to be one of the exceptions.

options.text: assumes that Dana's publisher is typical of all publishers
options.why: Even if her publisher is typical, "most" still doesn't guarantee Dana's result.

options.text: confuses earning back an advance with writing a good novel
options.why: Quality isn't discussed.

options.text: relies on statistics about advances that may be out of date
options.why: Nothing suggests the figures are outdated.

options.text: generalizes from a single novelist to all novelists
options.why: It runs the other way, applying a group statistic to one person.

items.tldr: "Most" makes Dana's outcome likely, not certain.

steps.label: Premise
steps.body: Most first-time novelists fall short.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: The conclusion says Dana definitely will, which needs "all."

items.takeaway: Statistical premises support probable conclusions, not certain ones.

items.stimulus: Each player on the Rockport team is among the most skilled players in the league. Therefore, the Rockport team will surely be one of the best teams in the league this season.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: relies on the opinion of the team's coach
options.why: No one's opinion is cited.

options.text: assumes that skill can be measured objectively
options.why: The argument takes the players' skill as given; measurement isn't the issue.

options.text: presumes that because each member of a group has a characteristic, the group as a whole must have it
options.why: Skilled individuals can still make a poor team if they don't play well together.

options.text: presumes that because a group has a characteristic, each member of the group must have it
options.why: That is the reverse direction. This argument runs from members to the group.

options.text: draws a conclusion about the whole league from one team
options.why: The conclusion is about one team.

items.tldr: Great players don't guarantee a great team. That's the part-to-whole flaw.

steps.label: Direction
steps.body: From each player (parts) to the team (whole).

steps.label: Gap
steps.body: A team's quality depends on how players combine, not just on each player alone.

items.takeaway: What's true of each part needn't be true of the whole (composition).

items.stimulus: A magazine invited readers to mail in a survey about job satisfaction. Of the 3,000 readers who responded, 80 percent said they were unhappy at work. Clearly, most of the magazine's readers are dissatisfied with their jobs.
items.prompt: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

options.text: assumes that job satisfaction can't change over time
options.why: The argument makes no claim about change.

options.text: fails to consider that readers who were unhappy at work may have been more likely than others to respond
options.why: A self-selected sample can overrepresent people with strong feelings about the topic.

options.text: confuses dissatisfaction with a job with dissatisfaction with a career
options.why: That distinction plays no role in the argument.

options.text: presumes that the magazine's editors designed the survey fairly
options.why: The survey's wording isn't the issue; the sample's selection is.

options.text: relies on a sample too small to draw any conclusion
options.why: Three thousand responses is a lot; the problem is who chose to respond.

items.tldr: Volunteers who chose to answer may be the unhappiest readers.

steps.label: Sample
steps.body: Readers who chose to mail back a survey.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: People with grievances are often more motivated to respond, so the sample is biased.

items.takeaway: Self-selected samples are suspect even when they are large.

items.stimulus: Senator Hale argues that the city should ban plastic shopping bags. But Senator Hale herself was photographed carrying groceries in plastic bags last month. So her argument should be rejected.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: rejects an argument because the person making it has acted inconsistently with it
options.why: Whether the ban is a good idea doesn't depend on the senator's own shopping habits.

options.text: relies on a photograph whose authenticity is doubtful
options.why: Nothing suggests the photo is fake, and its authenticity wouldn't matter anyway.

options.text: treats a single month as typical of the senator's behavior
options.why: Even years of plastic-bag use wouldn't refute her argument.

options.text: assumes that a ban on plastic bags would be easy to enforce
options.why: Enforcement is never discussed.

options.text: confuses what is legal with what is moral
options.why: The argument doesn't discuss legality or morality.

items.tldr: The senator's hypocrisy, if it is that, doesn't make her argument wrong.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: She uses plastic bags herself.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: That attacks the arguer, not the reasons for the ban.

items.takeaway: An argument can be sound even if its author doesn't live by it.

items.stimulus: The study found a statistically significant difference between the two groups' reading scores. A significant difference is an important difference. So the study found that the difference between the groups' reading scores is important.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: assumes that the study's sample was representative
options.why: Even a perfect sample wouldn't fix the shift in meaning.

options.text: relies on a study that may have been poorly designed
options.why: The argument's problem lies in how it reads the finding, not in the study.

options.text: shifts between a technical and an everyday meaning of a key term
options.why: Statistically significant means unlikely to be due to chance; it doesn't mean large or important.

options.text: confuses a cause of the difference with an effect of it
options.why: No causal claim is made.

options.text: draws a conclusion about individuals from data about groups
options.why: The conclusion is about the groups' scores.

items.tldr: "Significant" in statistics means unlikely to be chance, not important.

steps.label: Key word
steps.body: "Significant."

steps.label: Two senses
steps.body: The study uses the statistical sense; the conclusion uses the everyday sense.

items.takeaway: Technical terms with everyday cousins are classic equivocation traps.

items.stimulus: Reported bicycle thefts rose by 50 percent last year in Danbury but by only 10 percent in Easton. So bicycle theft is now a bigger problem in Danbury than in Easton.
items.prompt: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

options.text: presumes that bicycle theft will keep rising in both towns
options.why: The argument makes no prediction.

options.text: overlooks the possibility that Easton has far more bicycle thefts than Danbury despite its smaller increase
options.why: Danbury could have gone from 4 thefts to 6 while Easton went from 1,000 to 1,100.

options.text: relies on figures from only one year
options.why: More years wouldn't fix confusing a rate of increase with an amount.

options.text: fails to consider other kinds of theft
options.why: The conclusion is only about bicycle theft.

options.text: assumes that all bicycle thefts are reported
options.why: Underreporting doesn't address the gap between growth rates and totals.

items.tldr: A bigger percentage increase can start from a much smaller base.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Growth rates, 50% vs 10%.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Which town's problem is bigger now, which depends on actual numbers.

items.takeaway: Percent changes say nothing about size without the starting amounts.

items.stimulus: A ship needs a single captain whose orders are obeyed without debate. A nation is like a ship. So a nation should be ruled by a single leader whose orders are obeyed without debate.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: confuses a necessary condition for a sufficient one
options.why: No conditional reasoning is reversed.

options.text: assumes that what is true of one ship is true of all ships
options.why: The argument's weakness is the ship–nation comparison, not ship generalizations.

options.text: relies on an analogy without showing that the two things are alike in the respects that matter
options.why: Ships face emergencies needing instant obedience; nations differ in size, purpose and timescale.

options.text: concludes that something is true merely because it has not been disproved
options.why: The argument offers an analogy as positive support.

options.text: attacks those who favor debate rather than their arguments
options.why: No opponents are mentioned.

items.tldr: Calling a nation "like a ship" doesn't show they're alike in the ways that matter.

steps.label: Structure
steps.body: Ships need X; nations are like ships; so nations need X.

steps.label: Test the analogy
steps.body: Do the features that justify a captain's authority carry over to a nation? The argument never shows that.

items.takeaway: An analogy is only as strong as the relevant similarity between its two cases.

items.stimulus: The orchid will flower only if it gets at least six hours of sunlight a day. Since it is now getting eight hours of sunlight a day, it will flower.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: takes a condition required for flowering to be enough to make the orchid flower
options.why: "Only if" marks a necessary condition. The orchid might also need water, warmth or maturity.

options.text: assumes that more sunlight is always better for the orchid
options.why: The argument never claims eight hours beats six.

options.text: concludes that one event caused another because they occurred together
options.why: No correlation is offered as evidence.

options.text: relies on a measurement of sunlight that may be inaccurate
options.why: Nothing suggests the measurement is wrong.

options.text: overlooks the possibility that the orchid flowered in the past with less sunlight
options.why: The premise says it can't flower with less than six hours.

items.tldr: "Only if" gives a requirement, not a guarantee.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: Flowers → 6+ hours of sun. Has 8 hours, so the argument concludes it will flower.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: That reverses the conditional.

items.takeaway: "X only if Y" means X → Y. Having Y doesn't give you X.

items.stimulus: Any candidate who wins the teachers' union's endorsement will win the election. Morales did not win the union's endorsement. So Morales will not win the election.
items.prompt: The argument's reasoning is flawed because it

options.text: takes for granted that Morales sought the union's endorsement
options.why: Whether she sought it doesn't affect the logical gap.

options.text: treats the election's outcome as already decided
options.why: The real problem is the negated conditional, not certainty as such.

options.text: assumes that the union's endorsement is based on candidates' qualifications
options.why: The basis of the endorsement plays no role.

options.text: overlooks the possibility that a candidate could win the election without the union's endorsement
options.why: The endorsement guarantees a win, but nothing says it's the only path to one.

options.text: presumes that the union's members all vote alike
options.why: The premise states the endorsement's effect directly.
