items.tldr: Endorsement is enough to win, not required to win.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: Endorsed → wins. Not endorsed, so the argument concludes not wins.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: Negating both sides doesn't preserve a conditional.

items.takeaway: From "if X then Y" and "not X," nothing follows about Y.

items.stimulus: Cities with more police officers per resident tend to have higher crime rates. So hiring more police officers tends to increase crime.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: confuses violent crime with crime in general
options.why: No distinction between kinds of crime is drawn.

options.text: assumes that crime rates are reported accurately
options.why: Accurate reporting wouldn't fix the causal reversal.

options.text: generalizes from a small number of cities
options.why: The number of cities isn't given, and it isn't the main problem.

options.text: ignores the possibility that high crime rates lead cities to hire more police officers
options.why: The correlation fits causation running the other way.

options.text: relies on the testimony of police officials
options.why: No testimony is cited.

items.tldr: Crime may drive police hiring, rather than police driving crime.

steps.label: Claim
steps.body: More police → more crime.

steps.label: Alternative
steps.body: More crime → more police explains the same pattern.

items.takeaway: When a correlation is offered as cause, always test the reverse direction.

items.stimulus: We can trust this encyclopedia's account of the war, because the encyclopedia is reliable. And we know it is reliable because its accounts, including this one, are accurate.
items.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the argument?

options.text: It concludes that the account is accurate because no one has disproved it.
options.why: The argument offers a circular reason, not a lack of disproof.

options.text: It confuses the accuracy of an account with its completeness.
options.why: Completeness never comes up.

options.text: It uses the accuracy of the very account in question as evidence that the account can be trusted.
options.why: Reliability is supported by the account's accuracy, which is what the argument set out to show.

options.text: It relies on an encyclopedia written by people who were not historians.
options.why: Nothing is said about the authors.

options.text: It assumes that what is true of one encyclopedia is true of all of them.
options.why: Only this encyclopedia is discussed.

items.tldr: Trusting the account because it's accurate, to prove it's accurate, is circular.

steps.label: Trace
steps.body: Account trustworthy ← encyclopedia reliable ← its accounts, including this one, are accurate.

steps.label: Notice
steps.body: The last link assumes the conclusion.

items.takeaway: Watch for support that quietly includes the very claim being argued for.

items.stimulus: The defense has not proven that the defendant was somewhere else at the time of the robbery. Therefore, the defendant must have been at the scene.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: confuses the time of the robbery with its location
options.why: That confusion doesn't occur.

options.text: overlooks the possibility that the robbery never took place
options.why: Even granting the robbery happened, the inference still fails.

options.text: assumes that the defense attorney is incompetent
options.why: The attorney's skill isn't discussed.

options.text: relies on eyewitness testimony
options.why: No testimony is mentioned.

options.text: treats the failure to prove a claim as proof that the opposite claim is true
options.why: An unproven alibi doesn't place the defendant at the scene.

items.tldr: "No alibi" isn't "proof of presence."

steps.label: Premise
steps.body: No proof the defendant was elsewhere.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: The conclusion needs positive evidence of presence.

items.takeaway: Lack of evidence against a claim is not evidence for it.

items.stimulus: Housing experts predict that home prices in Millport will rise over the coming year. Therefore, anyone who buys a house in Millport this year will be able to sell it next year for more than they paid.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: treats a prediction about prices in general as guaranteeing the outcome of every individual purchase
options.why: A predicted overall rise is uncertain and can't ensure that each house gains value.

options.text: fails to consider that some people buy houses to live in rather than to sell
options.why: The conclusion concerns whether buyers could sell at a profit, not whether they want to.

options.text: relies on experts whose predictions concern a matter outside their expertise
options.why: Housing experts predicting housing prices are within their field.

options.text: assumes that home prices in Millport have risen in the past
options.why: Past prices aren't mentioned.

options.text: confuses a cause of rising prices with an effect of them
options.why: No causal claim is made.

items.tldr: A forecast for the market can't guarantee a profit on every house.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: A prediction about overall prices.

steps.label: Two leaps
steps.body: From predicted to certain, and from the market as a whole to every single house.

items.takeaway: Watch for conclusions that turn a general, uncertain trend into a guarantee for each case.

items.stimulus: My opponent says the school district should reduce its budget by two percent. But I will never support a plan that leaves our children without teachers or textbooks.
items.prompt: The reasoning above is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

options.text: relies on an emotional appeal to parents' concern for their children
options.why: The emotion rides on a distorted version of the proposal, which is the real flaw.

options.text: responds to a far more drastic proposal than the one the opponent actually made
options.why: A two percent cut is not a plan to eliminate teachers and textbooks.

options.text: assumes that teachers and textbooks are the district's only expenses
options.why: The speaker doesn't make that assumption explicitly; the flaw is the distortion.

options.text: attacks the opponent's character
options.why: The speaker attacks a position, though a misstated one.

options.text: fails to state how much the budget should be
options.why: The speaker needn't propose an alternative to be criticized for distortion.

items.tldr: A small cut is recast as a catastrophic one. That's a straw man.

steps.label: Actual proposal
steps.body: Cut the budget by 2%.

steps.label: Response
steps.body: Rejects a plan that would eliminate teachers and textbooks, which no one proposed.

items.takeaway: Compare the view being rebutted with the view actually stated.

items.stimulus: Most professional chess players began playing chess before the age of ten. So most people who begin playing chess before the age of ten go on to become professional chess players.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: fails to define what counts as a professional chess player
options.why: A precise definition wouldn't fix the reversal.

options.text: relies on a sample of chess players that is too small
options.why: The sample size isn't given, and the error is in the logic.

options.text: assumes that starting chess early causes a player to become a professional
options.why: The conclusion isn't causal; it reverses a "most" statement.

options.text: presumes that skill at chess is innate
options.why: Innate skill isn't discussed.

options.text: infers that most members of one group belong to a second group from the fact that most of the second group belong to the first
options.why: Most professionals started early, but millions start early and very few become professionals.

items.tldr: "Most pros started young" doesn't mean "most who start young become pros."

steps.label: Premise
steps.body: Most of group P (pros) are in group Q (early starters).

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Most of Q are in P, a reversal that ignores how much bigger Q is.

items.takeaway: "Most" statements don't reverse. Compare the sizes of the two groups.

items.stimulus: Every witness agrees that the robber was tall. But eyewitness testimony is notoriously unreliable. So the robber was probably not tall.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: confuses the robber's height with the robber's identity
options.why: Identity isn't discussed.

options.text: relies on a generalization about testimony that is clearly false
options.why: The generalization may be true; the problem is what's inferred from it.

options.text: takes evidence that a claim is poorly supported as evidence that the claim is false
options.why: Unreliable testimony weakens support for "tall" but gives no reason to think "not tall."

options.text: fails to consider that the witnesses may have discussed the robbery with one another
options.why: That would further weaken the testimony, but still wouldn't support "not tall."

options.text: assumes that all the witnesses saw the robber from the same distance
options.why: Viewing conditions aren't discussed.

items.tldr: Weak evidence for "tall" isn't evidence for "not tall."

steps.label: Premises
steps.body: Witnesses say tall; testimony is unreliable.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: At most, we're left not knowing. Nothing points toward "not tall."

items.takeaway: Undermining support for a claim leaves it unsupported, not refuted.

items.stimulus: The buildings that survive from ancient Rome are remarkably sturdy. Clearly, Roman builders built sturdier buildings than modern builders do.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: confuses sturdiness with beauty
options.why: Beauty isn't mentioned.

options.text: relies on the testimony of archaeologists
options.why: No testimony is cited.

options.text: overlooks the possibility that Rome's weaker buildings collapsed long ago, leaving only the sturdiest
options.why: The survivors are a biased sample of Roman construction.

options.text: fails to define what counts as a modern building
options.why: A definition wouldn't fix the biased sample.

options.text: assumes that modern buildings will last as long as Roman ones
options.why: The argument makes no prediction about modern buildings.

items.tldr: Only the sturdiest Roman buildings survived to be seen.

steps.label: Sample
steps.body: Roman buildings that still stand.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: Survival itself selects for sturdiness, so the sample isn't representative.

items.takeaway: Samples filtered by survival or success overstate how good the typical case was.

items.stimulus: The average household income in Brentwood is higher than the average household income in Carlisle. So the Ito household, which is in Brentwood, has a higher income than the Park household, which is in Carlisle.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: applies a comparison of group averages to particular members of the groups
options.why: Averages leave plenty of room for a low-income Brentwood household and a high-income Carlisle one.

options.text: overlooks the possibility that the two towns have different costs of living
options.why: Costs of living don't affect which household earns more.

options.text: relies on income figures that may be out of date
options.why: Nothing suggests the figures are outdated.

options.text: assumes that income is the best measure of well-being
options.why: The conclusion concerns income only.

options.text: generalizes from two households to two whole towns
options.why: It runs the other way, from towns to households.

items.tldr: Higher town averages don't decide any particular comparison.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Group averages.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: A claim about two specific households, which averages can't settle.

items.takeaway: Averages describe groups. They don't fix where any individual falls.

items.stimulus: Building the new subway line will cause years of construction noise for the residents of Elm District. Therefore, the city should not build the new subway line.
items.prompt: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

options.text: relies on the complaints of a few residents
options.why: No complaints are cited.

options.text: rejects a proposal because of one drawback without considering whether its benefits outweigh it
options.why: Faster commutes or less traffic might justify temporary noise; the argument never weighs them.

options.text: assumes that the construction noise will be permanent
options.why: The argument itself says the noise will last years, not forever.

options.text: confuses a cause of noise with an effect of noise
options.why: No such confusion occurs.

options.text: fails to specify where the subway line will run
options.why: The route isn't needed to see that the argument ignores benefits.

items.tldr: One cost alone can't settle whether a project is worth doing.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: One drawback, noise.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: A should-not conclusion needs costs and benefits compared.

items.takeaway: Recommendations based on a single cost or benefit ignore the other side of the ledger.

items.stimulus: Most of the car accidents in the county occur within five miles of the drivers' homes. So driving near home is more dangerous than driving far from home.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: presumes that all drivers in the county live in the county
options.why: Even if some don't, the argument's main gap remains.

options.text: assumes that accidents near home are less severe
options.why: Severity isn't discussed.

options.text: fails to consider that most driving may be done within five miles of home
options.why: If most miles are driven near home, most accidents would occur there even if it's no riskier.

options.text: confuses the cause of an accident with its location
options.why: Location is the focus, but causes aren't confused.

options.text: relies on accident reports that may be incomplete
options.why: Complete reports wouldn't fix the missing comparison of driving amounts.

items.tldr: More accidents near home may just reflect more driving near home.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: The share of accidents near home.

steps.label: Missing piece
steps.body: The share of driving near home. Risk is accidents per mile, not total accidents.

items.takeaway: Counts of bad outcomes mean little without how often each situation occurs.

items.stimulus: People who carry lighters are more likely than others to develop lung cancer. So carrying a lighter increases a person's risk of lung cancer.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: assumes that everyone who carries a lighter smokes
options.why: The argument assumes nothing about smoking; that is the factor it ignores.

options.text: presumes that cancer risk can be measured
options.why: Measuring risk isn't the problem; interpreting the correlation is.

options.text: relies on data from a single hospital
options.why: The data's source isn't mentioned.

options.text: overlooks the possibility that some other factor, such as smoking, explains both lighter carrying and lung cancer
options.why: Smokers carry lighters and get lung cancer more often; the lighter itself needn't do anything.

options.text: confuses lung cancer with other lung diseases
options.why: No other disease is mentioned.

items.tldr: Smoking explains both the lighter and the cancer.

steps.label: Correlation
steps.body: Lighter carriers get more lung cancer.

steps.label: Third factor
steps.body: Smoking leads to both.

items.takeaway: Look for a common cause before accepting that one correlated factor causes the other.

items.stimulus: Some members of the planning committee support the proposed zoning change. So some members of the planning committee do not support it.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: assumes that the committee will vote on the proposal
options.why: No vote is mentioned.

options.text: presumes that committee members always agree with one another
options.why: The conclusion claims some members disagree, the opposite of this.

options.text: relies on a sample of committee members that is unrepresentative
options.why: No sample is involved.

options.text: takes for granted that if some members of a group have a property, not all of them do
options.why: "Some" means at least one. All the members might support the change.

options.text: confuses supporting a proposal with voting for it
options.why: Voting isn't mentioned.

items.tldr: "Some" doesn't rule out "all."

steps.label: Premise
steps.body: At least one member supports it.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: That's compatible with every member supporting it, so "some don't" doesn't follow.

items.takeaway: In LSAT logic, "some" means "at least one, possibly all."

items.stimulus: Economists disagree about whether the proposed tax cut would increase economic growth. So no one can know whether it would, and the government should ignore economists' advice on the matter.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: infers from the fact that experts disagree that their views have no value at all
options.why: Disagreeing experts can still narrow the range of plausible outcomes and inform the decision.

options.text: treats a claim about economists as a claim about economics
options.why: The real leap is from disagreement to worthlessness.

options.text: relies on the opinion of a single economist
options.why: The argument cites disagreement among many economists.

options.text: assumes that the tax cut will pass
options.why: Passage of the tax cut isn't discussed.

options.text: confuses economic growth with employment
options.why: Employment isn't mentioned.

items.tldr: Expert disagreement doesn't make expert advice worthless.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Economists disagree.

steps.label: Two leaps
steps.body: That no one can know, and that their advice should be ignored entirely.

items.takeaway: Uncertainty calls for weighing expert views, not discarding them.

items.stimulus: The chance that any particular ticket will win the state lottery is one in ten million. So the person who won last week's lottery must have cheated.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: assumes that all lottery tickets cost the same
options.why: Ticket prices are irrelevant to the reasoning.

options.text: presumes that the winner bought only one ticket
options.why: Even a single ticket winning isn't evidence of cheating, given how many were sold.

options.text: relies on odds that are probably miscalculated
options.why: Nothing suggests the odds are wrong.

options.text: confuses the lottery's legality with its fairness
options.why: Neither legality nor fairness in that sense is discussed.

options.text: overlooks the fact that it was very likely some ticket would win, even though each ticket was unlikely to
options.why: With millions of tickets sold, someone winning is expected; one person's win isn't suspicious by itself.

items.tldr: Each ticket is a long shot, but some ticket winning is nearly certain.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Any one ticket has tiny odds.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: That's true of every ticket, yet someone had to win, so the winner's luck proves nothing.

items.takeaway: An unlikely outcome for each case can still be a likely outcome for some case.

items.stimulus: If people came to believe that free will is an illusion, many of them would behave less responsibly. Therefore, free will is not an illusion.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: generalizes from a few people to everyone
options.why: The premise concerns "many" people, and the flaw lies elsewhere.

options.text: confuses believing something with knowing it

items.stimulus: The new reading app must improve children's literacy. In the schools that adopted it this year, students' reading scores rose by 12 percent.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: The app was developed with input from experienced reading teachers.
options.why: Expert input, if anything, makes the app's effectiveness more plausible.

options.text: The app costs schools less than printed workbooks.
options.why: Cost doesn't bear on whether the app improves literacy.

options.text: Children who used the app reported enjoying it.
options.why: Enjoyment says nothing about whether the app raised scores.

options.text: A few children in the adopting schools showed no improvement.
options.why: An average rise is compatible with some children not improving.

options.text: The same schools also hired additional reading specialists this year.
options.why: The specialists offer a rival explanation for the higher scores.

items.tldr: Another change in the same schools could explain the gains.

steps.label: Argument
steps.body: The app was adopted and scores rose, so the argument concludes the app worked.

steps.label: Weaken
steps.body: Supply a rival cause that arrived at the same time.

items.takeaway: Rival causes that coincide with the proposed cause are the classic weakener.

items.stimulus: To reduce rush-hour traffic congestion downtown, the city will raise parking fees there. Higher fees will discourage people from driving downtown, so congestion will decrease.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: Parking fees in nearby cities are higher than the city's new fees.
options.why: Other cities' fees don't affect how drivers here will respond.

options.text: Most of the cars on downtown streets at rush hour are passing through on their way elsewhere and never park downtown.
options.why: Parking fees can't change the behavior of drivers who don't park, and they cause most of the congestion.

options.text: Some downtown workers already take the bus.
options.why: That doesn't show the fees won't discourage those who still drive and park.

options.text: The city will spend the extra fee revenue on road repairs.
options.why: How the revenue is spent doesn't affect congestion now.

options.text: Downtown merchants oppose the fee increase.
options.why: Opposition doesn't show the plan won't reduce congestion.

items.tldr: Fees can't deter drivers who don't park downtown.

steps.label: Plan
steps.body: Raise parking fees, deter drivers, reduce congestion.

steps.label: Weaken
steps.body: Show that the people causing congestion aren't affected by the plan.

items.takeaway: A plan is weakened when its lever doesn't reach the main source of the problem.

items.stimulus: Children who eat dinner with their families most nights are less likely than other children to use illegal drugs as teenagers. So families that want to keep their children away from drugs should eat dinner together.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the argument?

options.text: Parents who hold nightly family dinners also tend to monitor their children's activities closely, and close monitoring itself reduces teenage drug use.
options.why: If monitoring is what protects children, family dinners alone wouldn't help.

options.text: Family dinners are more common in households with younger children.
options.why: The age of children at dinner doesn't explain the link to later drug use.

options.text: Children who eat with their families tend to have healthier diets.
options.why: Diet is another benefit of family dinners, not a challenge to the argument.

options.text: Family dinners have become less common over the past few decades.
options.why: How common dinners are doesn't affect whether they reduce drug use.

options.text: Some teenagers who ate dinner with their families still used drugs.
options.why: The claim is about reduced likelihood, which allows exceptions.

items.tldr: A third factor, parental monitoring, may produce both the dinners and the lower drug use.

steps.label: Argument
steps.body: The correlation leads to a recommendation to eat together.

steps.label: Weaken
steps.body: A common cause means the recommended action may not work on its own.

items.takeaway: Recommendations based on correlations are weakened by a common cause.

items.stimulus: A survey of members of the city's gyms found that 80 percent want the city to build more bike paths. So most of the city's residents want more bike paths.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: Some gym members did not answer the bike-path question.
options.why: A few skipped questions don't show the sample is unrepresentative.

options.text: Gym members in the city are far more likely than other residents to ride bicycles.
options.why: The sample overrepresents cyclists, so its enthusiasm for bike paths may not reflect residents generally.

options.text: Building bike paths would be expensive.
options.why: Cost doesn't tell us what residents want.

options.text: Most of the gym members surveyed live in the city.
options.why: That makes the sample more relevant to residents, if anything.

options.text: The survey was conducted in the spring.
options.why: The season alone gives no clear reason to think the results are skewed.

items.tldr: Gym members are likelier to be cyclists than residents in general.

steps.label: Sample
steps.body: Gym members.

steps.label: Weaken
steps.body: Show the sample differs from residents in a way that matters for the question.

items.takeaway: To weaken a survey argument, show the sample is biased on exactly the issue asked about.

items.stimulus: Talking on a hands-free phone while driving is no more dangerous than talking with a passenger, since both involve the same kind of conversation. So drivers should be allowed to use hands-free phones.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: Hands-free phones are more expensive than handheld phones.
options.why: Price is irrelevant to safety.

options.text: Some drivers find conversations with passengers distracting.
options.why: If passenger talk is also distracting, the analogy is untouched; it just lowers both.

options.text: Many drivers already use hands-free phones.
options.why: How common the practice is doesn't show whether it's safe.

options.text: Passengers tend to stop talking when traffic becomes demanding, but people on the phone cannot see the road and keep talking.
options.why: This is a relevant difference between the two conversations, so the analogy fails.

options.text: Talking with a passenger is less dangerous than texting while driving.
options.why: The comparison with texting doesn't affect the comparison the argument makes.

items.tldr: Passengers adjust to traffic; callers can't. The analogy breaks.

steps.label: Analogy
steps.body: Phone talk is like passenger talk, so it should be equally acceptable.

steps.label: Weaken
steps.body: Find a relevant way the two differ.

items.takeaway: Analogies are weakened by a relevant difference between the compared cases.

items.stimulus: Most people struck by lightning are men. So there must be some physical difference between men and women that makes men more likely to be struck by lightning.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: Most people struck by lightning survive.
options.why: Survival rates don't explain who gets struck.

options.text: Men are much more likely than women to work and spend leisure time outdoors during thunderstorms.
options.why: Greater exposure explains the pattern without any physical difference.

options.text: Lightning safety campaigns are aimed at both men and women.
options.why: Campaigns aimed at both groups don't explain a difference between them.

options.text: Lightning strikes are more common in summer than in winter.
options.why: Seasonal patterns affect men and women alike.

options.text: Men are, on average, taller than women.
options.why: Height is a physical difference, so this could support the argument.

items.tldr: Exposure, not physiology, can explain who gets struck.

steps.label: Argument
steps.body: More men are struck, so the argument concludes men's bodies must differ.

steps.label: Weaken
steps.body: Offer a difference in exposure instead.

items.takeaway: Differences in outcomes often reflect differences in exposure, not in the groups themselves.

items.stimulus: Since the city began adding fluoride to its water ten years ago, tooth decay among its children has dropped by half. Fluoridation, then, is responsible for the decline.

options.why: If decay fell just as much without fluoride, something other than fluoridation drove the decline.

options.text: Some residents of the city drink only bottled water.
options.why: A few residents avoiding tap water doesn't undercut the citywide effect.

options.text: Tooth decay among adults in the city also declined.
options.why: That's consistent with fluoridated water helping everyone.

options.why: Toothpaste fluoride doesn't by itself show that the water fluoride did nothing.

items.tldr: The same decline without fluoride points to another cause.

steps.label: Argument
steps.body: Fluoride came, decay fell, so the argument credits fluoride.

steps.label: Weaken
steps.body: A comparison group without fluoride saw the same decline.

items.takeaway: A matching change where the proposed cause is absent undercuts the causal claim.

steps.label: Weaken

items.takeaway: Weaken a prediction by cutting the connection between its evidence and its outcome.

items.stimulus: Archaeologists have found that nearly every house in the ancient city of Tessa had a large cistern for storing rainwater. This shows that Tessa's climate was dry.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: Some of Tessa's cisterns were larger than others.
options.why: Variation in size doesn't bear on the climate.

options.text: Other ancient cities in the region also had cisterns.
options.why: That's consistent with the whole region being dry.

options.text: Tessa's houses were built mostly of stone.
options.why: Building materials don't explain the cisterns.

options.text: Cisterns were expensive to build.
options.why: Costly cisterns suggest residents badly needed stored water, which fits a dry climate.

options.text: Tessa's river was heavily polluted by the city's many tanneries, making its water unsafe to drink.
options.why: Polluted river water gives residents a reason to store rainwater even in a wet climate.

items.tldr: Polluted rivers, not a dry climate, could explain the cisterns.

steps.label: Argument
steps.body: Cisterns everywhere, so the argument concludes the climate was dry.

steps.label: Weaken
steps.body: Give another reason people would store rainwater.

items.takeaway: When an argument explains evidence one way, a weakener offers another explanation.

items.stimulus: After the Dalton Mall installed security cameras, shoplifting there fell by 30 percent. So installing cameras in all of the city's malls would reduce shoplifting in the city.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: Some shoplifters at the Dalton Mall were caught on camera.
options.why: That supports the cameras' usefulness.

options.text: The cameras at the Dalton Mall were expensive to install.
options.why: Cost doesn't affect whether cameras reduce shoplifting.

options.text: After the Dalton Mall installed its cameras, shoplifting rose by a similar amount at stores without cameras nearby.
options.why: If shoplifters simply moved elsewhere, cameras shift shoplifting rather than reducing it citywide.

options.text: Shoplifting at the Dalton Mall had been rising before the cameras were installed.
options.why: A rising trend that reversed makes the cameras' effect look stronger.

options.text: The Dalton Mall is the largest mall in the city.
options.why: Size alone doesn't show the effect wouldn't repeat elsewhere.

items.tldr: If shoplifting just moved, cameras don't cut the city's total.

steps.label: Argument
steps.body: Cameras cut shoplifting at one mall, so cameras everywhere would cut it citywide.

steps.label: Weaken
steps.body: Show the effect was displacement, not reduction.

items.takeaway: Local successes can hide displacement; check whether the problem simply moved.

items.stimulus: In a large study, people who drank three or more cups of coffee a day lived longer, on average, than people who drank no coffee. So drinking coffee extends life.

options.text: Tea drinkers in the study also lived longer than average.
options.why: That says nothing about why coffee drinkers outlived non-drinkers.

options.text: Some participants drank more than six cups of coffee a day.
options.why: Heavy drinkers' existence doesn't explain the difference between groups.

options.text: Coffee contains several compounds that act as antioxidants.
options.why: That suggests a way coffee might help, strengthening the argument.

options.text: Many of the study's participants who drank no coffee had given it up on their doctors' advice because of serious heart conditions.
options.why: The no-coffee group included many sick people, which explains their shorter lives without coffee doing anything.

options.text: The study included participants from several countries.
options.why: A diverse sample doesn't introduce a bias.

items.tldr: The no-coffee group was sicker to begin with.

steps.label: Argument
steps.body: Coffee drinkers lived longer, so the argument concludes coffee extends life.

steps.label: Weaken
steps.body: Show the comparison group differed in a way that explains the result.

items.takeaway: A group defined by not doing something may include people who stopped for health reasons.

items.stimulus: When Norland banned single-use plastic bags, plastic litter on its beaches fell by half. So a similar ban in Southport would cut plastic litter on Southport's beaches by half.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: Southport's beaches are larger than Norland's.
options.why: Size alone doesn't show the ban would work differently.

options.text: Norland's ban took effect three years ago.
options.why: The timing of Norland's ban doesn't affect the comparison.

options.text: Norland's ban was popular with its residents.
options.why: Popularity in Norland doesn't affect the outcome in Southport.

options.text: Most of the plastic litter on Southport's beaches washes ashore from fishing boats rather than coming from shoppers.
options.why: A bag ban targets shoppers, so it can't cut litter that mostly comes from fishing boats.

options.text: Plastic bags harm sea turtles and other wildlife.
options.why: Harm to wildlife doesn't bear on how much litter the ban would remove.

steps.label: Analogy
steps.body: It worked in Norland, so it will work the same way in Southport.

steps.label: Weaken
steps.body: Show a relevant difference in where the litter comes from.

items.takeaway: Transferring a result between places assumes the places are alike in the relevant way.

items.stimulus: Since the city installed speed cameras on Harbor Road, the number of speeding tickets issued there has risen sharply. So the cameras have failed to reduce speeding on Harbor Road.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: Speeding tickets on nearby roads also increased.
options.why: That doesn't explain why tickets on Harbor Road rose.

options.text: Before the cameras were installed, police rarely patrolled Harbor Road, so few speeders were ever ticketed.
options.why: More tickets can reflect far better detection, even if speeding itself declined.

options.text: Some drivers on Harbor Road were ticketed more than once.
options.why: Repeat offenders suggest the cameras didn't deter some drivers.

options.text: The cameras cost the city a great deal to install.
options.why: Cost doesn't bear on whether speeding fell.

options.text: Speed cameras are used in many other cities.
options.why: Use elsewhere says nothing about speeding on Harbor Road.

items.tldr: More tickets may mean more detection, not more speeding.

steps.label: Argument
steps.body: Tickets rose, so the argument concludes speeding didn't fall.

steps.label: Weaken
steps.body: Tickets measure detection as well as speeding; detection jumped.

items.takeaway: Counts of detected events depend on how hard anyone was looking.

items.stimulus: In our survey, 70 percent of respondents said they would buy a fully electric pickup truck. So electric pickups will soon make up a majority of pickup truck sales.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: Some respondents already own electric cars.
options.why: That doesn't show their intentions are unreliable.

options.text: In past surveys, far fewer people bought new kinds of vehicles than said they would.
options.why: If stated intentions overstate purchases, the 70 percent figure won't translate into sales.

options.text: The survey was conducted online.
options.why: An online survey isn't, by itself, shown to be biased on this question.

options.text: Electric pickups can tow heavy loads.
options.why: A useful feature makes sales more likely.

options.text: Several manufacturers plan to release electric pickups next year.
options.why: More supply makes higher sales more plausible.

items.tldr: People's stated buying plans have overstated real purchases.

steps.label: Argument
steps.body: Stated intent, so the argument predicts actual sales.

steps.label: Weaken
steps.body: Show that intent poorly predicts behavior.

items.takeaway: Survey answers about future behavior are weak evidence; history of the gap weakens them further.

items.stimulus: Students who take private music lessons score higher on math tests than students who do not. So music lessons improve math skills.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: Music involves counting beats and recognizing patterns.
options.why: That suggests a way music might help math, strengthening the argument.

options.text: Music lessons are offered at many schools.
options.why: Availability doesn't affect the causal claim.

options.text: Math tests measure only some mathematical skills.
options.why: The argument concerns the skills the tests measure; this doesn't undercut the link.

options.text: Some students who take music lessons dislike math.
options.why: Dislike doesn't undercut the score difference.

options.text: Most families that pay for music lessons also pay for math tutoring.
options.why: Tutoring is a rival explanation for the higher math scores.

items.tldr: Tutoring, which comes with the same families, could explain the scores.

steps.label: Argument
steps.body: Music students score higher, so the argument concludes music helps math.

steps.label: Weaken
steps.body: Supply a factor that comes with music lessons and boosts math directly.

items.takeaway: Look for something that travels with the proposed cause and could produce the effect.

items.stimulus: Sales of the store's organic produce have doubled over the past year. Clearly, shoppers are increasingly willing to pay more for organic food.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: Organic farming uses fewer synthetic pesticides.
options.why: Farming methods don't address shoppers' willingness to pay.

options.text: The store advertised its organic produce more heavily.
options.why: Advertising could boost sales while shoppers still pay more.

options.text: The store's sales of conventional produce stayed the same.
options.why: That doesn't explain why organic sales rose.

options.text: Over the past year, the store cut its prices for organic produce to match those for conventional produce.
options.why: If organic produce no longer costs more, rising sales show nothing about willingness to pay more.

options.text: Several new customers began shopping at the store this year.
options.why: New customers could still be paying a premium for organic food.

items.tldr: Sales can't show willingness to pay more if the price premium vanished.

steps.label: Argument
steps.body: Organic sales doubled, so the argument concludes shoppers will pay more.

steps.label: Weaken
steps.body: Remove the premium, and rising sales say nothing about paying more.

items.takeaway: Check whether the evidence actually involves the thing the conclusion is about.

items.stimulus: The diary of a nineteenth-century sailor describes a violent storm that wrecked a merchant ship off the coast of Alder Point in 1854. So a merchant ship was wrecked off Alder Point that year.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: The diary was written decades after the voyage, and many of the other events it describes are known to have been invented.
options.why: This undermines the diary as a source for any event it reports.

options.text: The sailor later became a ship's captain.
options.why: His later career doesn't affect the diary's reliability.

options.text: Storms were common off Alder Point in the 1850s.
options.why: That makes a wreck there more plausible.

options.text: Several merchant ships sailed past Alder Point in 1854.
options.why: More ships nearby makes a wreck slightly more plausible.

options.text: The diary is now kept in a museum.
options.why: Where it's kept doesn't bear on its accuracy.

items.tldr: An unreliable source can't establish the wreck.

steps.label: Argument
steps.body: The diary says it happened, so the argument concludes it happened.

steps.label: Weaken
steps.body: Undermine the source's reliability.

items.takeaway: When a conclusion rests on one source, attack the source.

items.stimulus: Two years ago the city raised its tax on hotel rooms, and since then the number of conventions held in the city has fallen sharply. Clearly, the higher tax has driven conventions away.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: Hotel taxes in other cities are lower than this city's tax.
options.why: That would make the city less attractive, supporting the argument.

options.text: The city's only large convention center has been closed for renovation for the past two years.
options.why: The closure explains the drop in conventions without the tax.

options.text: The tax revenue has been used to improve city parks.
options.why: How the revenue is spent doesn't affect the causal claim.

options.text: Some conventions held in the city before the tax increase were small.
options.why: Their size doesn't explain why conventions declined.

options.text: Tourists who are not attending conventions also stay in the city's hotels.
options.why: Other hotel guests don't bear on why conventions fell.

items.tldr: The convention center closed, which explains the drop by itself.

steps.label: Argument
steps.body: Tax rose, conventions fell, so the argument blames the tax.

steps.label: Weaken
steps.body: A simultaneous rival cause.

items.takeaway: Before/after evidence is weakened by anything else that changed at the same time.

items.stimulus: In a clinical trial, 60 percent of patients who took an herbal remedy for headaches reported that their headaches improved. So the remedy is effective against headaches.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: The remedy is sold in many pharmacies.
options.why: Availability isn't evidence about effectiveness.

options.text: In a similar trial, 60 percent of patients given a sugar pill reported that their headaches improved.
options.why: The remedy did no better than a placebo, so the improvement isn't evidence of its effect.

options.text: Some patients in the trial had migraines.
options.why: Mixed headache types don't undercut the reported improvement.

options.text: Patients in the trial were not told what the remedy contained.
options.why: That doesn't show the improvement came from anything other than the remedy.

options.text: The herbal remedy has been used for centuries.
options.why: Long use doesn't show effectiveness.

items.tldr: A placebo produced the same improvement.

steps.label: Argument
steps.body: Most patients improved, so the argument calls the remedy effective.

steps.label: Weaken
steps.body: Without a control, improvement could be placebo or natural recovery; the sugar pill shows exactly that.

items.takeaway: Claims of effectiveness need a comparison with no treatment or a placebo.

items.stimulus: To increase use of the campus library, the board plans to keep it open until midnight. Many students have said they would use the library more if it stayed open later.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously calls into question the board's plan?

options.text: The library's study rooms are often full in the afternoon.
options.why: Crowding suggests demand that later hours might relieve.

options.text: Some students prefer to study in their rooms.
options.why: Some students staying home doesn't show later hours won't increase use.

options.text: The library has more books than any other in the region.
options.why: The size of the collection doesn't affect late-night use.

options.text: Students who study late often drink coffee.
options.why: Study habits like this don't bear on the plan.

options.text: When the library tried staying open until midnight last year, almost no one visited after ten o'clock.
options.why: A direct trial showed late hours didn't bring students in.

items.tldr: A past trial of late hours drew almost no one.

steps.label: Plan
steps.body: Later hours, supported by what students say they'd do.

steps.label: Weaken
steps.body: What students actually did when the hours were tried.

items.takeaway: Evidence of actual behavior trumps stated intentions.

items.stimulus: The number of people diagnosed with a particular sleep disorder has risen sharply over the past thirty years. So the disorder has become much more common over that time.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: The disorder can be treated effectively with medication.
options.why: Treatment doesn't bear on how common the disorder is.

options.text: The population has grown slightly over the past thirty years.
options.why: Slight growth can't explain a sharp rise.

options.text: Over the past thirty years, the criteria for diagnosing the disorder have been broadened, and doctors have become much more aware of it.
options.why: More diagnoses can come from broader criteria and awareness rather than more cases.

options.text: People with the disorder often feel tired during the day.
options.why: Symptoms don't explain the trend in diagnoses.

options.text: The disorder affects both children and adults.
options.why: Who is affected doesn't explain the rise.

items.tldr: Broader criteria and awareness can raise diagnoses without more cases.

steps.label: Argument
steps.body: More diagnoses, so the argument concludes there are more cases.

steps.label: Weaken
steps.body: Diagnosis rates also depend on how the condition is defined and noticed.

items.takeaway: A rise in diagnoses can reflect changes in diagnosis, not in the condition.

items.stimulus: Ninety percent of the customers who filled out our feedback form said they were satisfied with their purchases. So our customers are overwhelmingly satisfied.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: Customer satisfaction is important to the company's success.
options.why: Importance doesn't bear on whether the result is accurate.

options.text: The feedback form takes only a minute to complete.
options.why: A short form makes it easier for everyone to respond, reducing bias.

options.text: The company sells a wide range of products.
options.why: Product range doesn't affect the survey's representativeness.

options.text: The feedback form is given only to customers who return to make a second purchase.
options.why: Repeat buyers are likely to be satisfied, so the sample overstates satisfaction.

options.text: Some customers who were satisfied did not fill out the form.
options.why: That would mean satisfaction is, if anything, underestimated.

items.tldr: Only repeat customers, who are likely happy, got the form.

steps.label: Sample
steps.body: People who filled out the form.

steps.label: Weaken
steps.body: Show the form reached a group biased toward satisfaction.

items.takeaway: Feedback samples are often filtered toward happy customers.

items.stimulus: Plants grown in the east wing of the greenhouse, which were watered with a new fertilizer solution, grew taller than plants of the same species in the west wing, which received plain water. So the fertilizer promotes plant growth.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: The fertilizer contains nitrogen, which plants need to grow.
options.why: That suggests how the fertilizer could help.

options.text: The new fertilizer is more expensive than older fertilizers.
options.why: Price doesn't bear on whether it works.

options.text: The plants in both wings were planted on the same day.
options.why: That removes one possible difference, strengthening the comparison.

options.text: A few plants in the east wing did not grow taller than the west wing's average.
options.why: Exceptions don't undercut an average difference.

options.text: The east wing receives several more hours of direct sunlight each day than the west wing.
options.why: More sunlight could explain the extra growth without the fertilizer.

items.tldr: Extra sunlight, not fertilizer, may explain the taller plants.

steps.label: Argument
steps.body: Fertilized plants grew taller, so the argument credits the fertilizer.

steps.label: Weaken
steps.body: Another difference between the wings could explain the result.

items.takeaway: Comparisons are weakened by any other difference between the groups.

items.stimulus: The Hawks have won their last ten games against the Eagles. So the Hawks will win tomorrow's game against the Eagles.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: Tickets for tomorrow's game have sold out.
options.why: Ticket sales don't bear on the outcome.

options.text: The Eagles have a new team logo this season.
options.why: A logo doesn't affect who wins.

options.text: The Hawks have also won most of their games against other teams.
options.why: That suggests the Hawks are strong, supporting the prediction.

options.text: Tomorrow's game will be played at the Eagles' home stadium.
options.why: Without more, home field doesn't clearly offset ten straight wins.

options.text: The Hawks' three best players were injured this week and will not play tomorrow.
options.why: The team that won those games won't be the team playing tomorrow.

items.tldr: The winning streak came from players who won't be playing.

steps.label: Argument
steps.body: Past wins, so the argument predicts another win.

steps.label: Weaken
steps.body: Show that what produced the past wins has changed.

items.takeaway: Predictions from a track record assume the conditions behind it still hold.

items.stimulus: Switching the company's delivery fleet to electric vans will save money, because electricity costs far less per mile than gasoline.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: Electric vans produce no tailpipe emissions.
options.why: Emissions don't bear on whether the switch saves money.

options.text: Some of the company's drivers prefer gasoline vans.
options.why: Preferences don't affect costs.

options.text: Electricity prices have been stable for several years.
options.why: Stable prices make the fuel savings more reliable.

options.text: Electric vans cost so much more to buy that the fuel savings would not make up the difference within the vans' expected lifespan.
options.why: Then the switch costs more overall, despite cheaper fuel.

options.text: Gasoline prices rose last year.
options.why: Higher gasoline prices increase the savings from switching.

items.tldr: Higher purchase costs can outweigh fuel savings.

steps.label: Argument
steps.body: Cheaper fuel per mile, so the argument predicts savings overall.

steps.label: Weaken
steps.body: Bring in a cost the argument ignores.

items.takeaway: Savings claims based on one cost are weakened by a larger cost elsewhere.

items.stimulus: Residents of Marlow who drink at least two cups of green tea a day report fewer colds than residents who do not. Therefore, drinking green tea strengthens the immune system.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: Green tea contains antioxidants that have shown health benefits in laboratory studies.
options.why: If anything this supports the argument. A weakener has to attack the link between the tea and the colds.

options.text: Coffee drinkers in Marlow report more colds than green tea drinkers do.
options.why: Coffee drinkers are a new group. Comparing them can't explain why tea drinkers get fewer colds.

options.text: Some residents who drink green tea daily still report catching colds.
options.why: The claim is that tea drinkers get fewer colds, not none. A few colds don't contradict it.

options.text: Marlow residents who drink green tea daily are also far more likely to exercise regularly and sleep at least seven hours a night.
options.why: It offers a rival cause for the fewer colds, so the tea may be a bystander.

options.text: The survey of Marlow residents was conducted during the winter.
options.why: Winter affects both groups alike, so it can't explain the gap between them.

items.tldr: A rival cause (exercise, sleep) explains the gap, not the tea.

steps.label: Task
steps.body: Weaken. Find the fact that most undermines the conclusion.

steps.label: Core
steps.body: Evidence: tea drinkers report fewer colds. Conclusion: tea strengthens immunity.

steps.label: Gap
steps.body: A correlation is treated as a cause. Prephrase: something else about tea drinkers keeps colds away.

items.takeaway: Arguments that jump from correlation to cause fall to a rival cause that differs between the groups.

items.stimulus: Over the past decade, the districts of Halverton with the most public libraries have had the lowest rates of juvenile crime. So building additional libraries in the districts with the highest rates of juvenile crime would reduce juvenile crime in those districts.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: Juvenile crime in Halverton as a whole has declined over the past decade.
options.why: A citywide decline says nothing about why some districts have lower rates than others.

options.text: Most of Halverton's libraries were built more than thirty years ago.
options.why: The age of the buildings has no bearing on whether libraries reduce crime.

options.text: Some districts of Halverton with few public libraries also have low rates of juvenile crime.
options.why: A few exceptions don't undo a general pattern, and they don't show that libraries are irrelevant.

options.text: Libraries throughout Halverton have extended their evening hours in recent years.
options.why: The change applies to every district, so it can't account for differences between them.

options.text: The districts of Halverton with the most public libraries also have the highest household incomes and the most after-school programs.
options.why: Income and after-school programs are rival explanations for the low crime, so adding libraries alone might change nothing.

items.tldr: Wealth and after-school programs could explain the low crime, so more libraries may not help.

steps.label: Task
steps.body: Weaken a prediction that rests on a correlation.

steps.label: Core
steps.body: Evidence: more libraries go with less juvenile crime. Conclusion: adding libraries will cut crime.

steps.label: Gap
steps.body: It assumes the libraries cause the low crime. Prephrase: something else about those districts keeps crime low.

items.takeaway: When a plan copies one feature of a successful group, look for the other features that group has.

items.stimulus: Patients at Elmridge Clinic who used a new mobile reminder app took their medication on schedule far more consistently than patients who did not use the app. The clinic's director concludes that the app causes patients to take their medication more consistently.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the director's argument?

options.text: Before the app was introduced, the patients who later chose to use it had been no more consistent in taking their medication than other patients.
options.why: It rules out the main alternative: that the app users were already the more consistent patients.

options.text: Many clinics other than Elmridge have also begun recommending mobile reminder apps.
options.why: Other clinics' recommendations aren't evidence about this app's effect.

options.text: Patients who did not use the app were more likely to report unpleasant side effects from their medication.
options.why: That's a rival reason the non-users skipped doses, so it weakens the argument.

options.text: The app was developed by a company that also manufactures medication.
options.why: Who made the app says nothing about whether it changes patients' behavior.

options.text: Some patients who used the app nonetheless missed several doses of their medication.
options.why: The claim is about consistency compared with other patients. Some missed doses are expected either way.

items.tldr: Showing both groups started out equally consistent rules out self-selection.

steps.label: Task
steps.body: Strengthen a causal conclusion drawn from a comparison.

steps.label: Core
steps.body: App users were more consistent than non-users, so the app caused the consistency.

steps.label: Gap
steps.body: The users chose the app. Maybe the more conscientious patients are the ones who chose it.

steps.label: Fix
steps.body: Show the two groups were alike before the app arrived.

items.takeaway: To strengthen "X caused the difference," show the groups were alike before X.

items.stimulus: Critic: The novel Tidewater should not be assigned in introductory literature courses. Its plot turns on several historical events that most first-year students have never heard of, so those students would miss the point of the novel's central conflict.
items.prompt: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the critic's argument depends?

options.text: Tidewater is the only novel whose plot turns on unfamiliar historical events.
options.why: Other novels could share the problem. The argument doesn't depend on Tidewater being unique.

options.text: Advanced literature courses are a better place for novels with complex plots.
options.why: The critic never says where the novel should be assigned, so this isn't required.

options.text: Novels assigned in introductory literature courses should contain no historical references at all.
options.why: The argument doesn't need to ban every reference, only the kind that blocks understanding.

options.text: Most first-year students would enjoy Tidewater if they understood its historical references.
options.why: The argument is about understanding the conflict, not enjoyment.

options.text: Tidewater does not itself provide enough information about those historical events for an unfamiliar reader to grasp its central conflict.
options.why: Negate it: if the novel explains the events itself, students wouldn't miss the point and the argument collapses.

items.tldr: If the novel explained the history itself, students wouldn't miss the point, so the argument needs it not to.

steps.label: Task
steps.body: Necessary assumption. Find what the argument can't survive without.

steps.label: Core
steps.body: Evidence: students don't know the history. Conclusion: they'd miss the novel's point, so don't assign it.

steps.label: Gap
steps.body: Not knowing history beforehand only matters if the book doesn't fill it in.

steps.label: Check
steps.body: Negate the answer. If Tidewater explains the events, the argument fails.

items.takeaway: Use the negation test. A necessary assumption, once negated, breaks the argument.

items.stimulus: Anyone who qualifies for the Morrow Fellowship has published original research. Dana has not published any original research. Therefore, Dana is not eligible for the faculty travel grant.
items.prompt: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

options.text: Only people who qualify for the Morrow Fellowship are eligible for the faculty travel grant.
options.why: Grant → Fellowship → published. Dana hasn't published, so Dana can't qualify, so Dana isn't eligible.

options.text: Anyone who has published original research is eligible for the faculty travel grant.
options.why: This tells us who is eligible, not who isn't. It can't rule Dana out.

options.text: Anyone who qualifies for the Morrow Fellowship is eligible for the faculty travel grant.
options.why: That's Fellowship → grant, the wrong direction. We need grant → Fellowship.

options.text: Dana has applied for the Morrow Fellowship in the past.
options.why: Applying says nothing about qualifying or about the grant.

options.text: Most people who are eligible for the faculty travel grant have published original research.
options.why: "Most" leaves room for Dana to be eligible anyway, so the conclusion isn't guaranteed.

items.tldr: If only Fellowship-qualified people can get the grant, Dana (unpublished, so not qualified) can't get it.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: Premise: Fellowship → published. Contrapositive: not published → not Fellowship.

steps.label: Apply
steps.body: Dana hasn't published, so Dana doesn't qualify for the Fellowship.

steps.label: Gap
steps.body: The conclusion is about the travel grant, a new term. We need: not Fellowship → not grant, which is the same as grant → Fellowship.

items.takeaway: "Only X are Y" means Y → X. In sufficient assumption questions, the right answer chains the new term to the premises in the needed direction.

items.stimulus: Every successful restaurant in Lindale advertises on local radio. Café Orla advertises on local radio, so it will surely be successful.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument

options.text: assumes that what is true of restaurants in Lindale is true of restaurants everywhere
options.why: The conclusion stays in Lindale; it never generalizes beyond it.

options.text: confuses a cause of a restaurant's success with an effect of it
options.why: The argument makes no causal claim, only a conditional one, so this isn't the mistake.

options.text: relies on too small a sample of restaurants to support a general conclusion
options.why: The premise covers every successful restaurant. Sample size isn't the issue.

options.text: takes for granted that a condition required for success is enough to guarantee it
options.why: Radio ads are necessary for success in Lindale, not sufficient. Plenty of failing restaurants might advertise too.

options.text: attacks the reputation of Café Orla instead of evaluating its advertising
options.why: The argument says nothing about Café Orla's reputation.

items.tldr: Advertising is required for success, but the argument treats it as a guarantee.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: Premise: successful → advertises. The argument concludes: advertises → successful.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: That reverses the conditional, treating a necessary condition as a sufficient one.

items.takeaway: "All successful X do Y" never means "doing Y makes X successful."

items.stimulus: Each of the five programs in the Kestrel software suite runs quickly on older computers. So the Kestrel suite, with all five programs running at once, will run quickly on older computers.
items.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the argument?

options.text: It relies on testimony from the software's developers.
options.why: No testimony appears in the argument.

options.text: It treats one possible cause of slow performance as the only cause.
options.why: The argument never identifies a cause of slowness.

options.text: It draws a conclusion about all computers from evidence about older computers.
options.why: The conclusion is about older computers only.

options.text: It presumes that what is true of a whole is true of each of its parts.
options.why: That's the division flaw, the mirror image. Here the reasoning runs part → whole.

options.text: It presumes that what is true of each part of a whole is true of the whole.
options.why: Programs that are fast alone can be slow together, since they compete for the same memory and processor.

items.tldr: Five fast programs can still be slow when they run together.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: Each part (program) is fast, so the whole (the suite running together) must be fast.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: That's composition: properties of parts don't automatically transfer to the whole.

items.takeaway: Composition assumes parts → whole. Division assumes whole → parts. Both are flaws.

items.stimulus: Every Brennan College student who studies abroad must first complete two years of a foreign language. Of the Brennan students who were eligible to study abroad this year, fewer than half chose to do so. Even so, the number of Brennan students studying abroad this year is the highest in the college's history.
items.prompt: If the statements above are true, which one of the following is most strongly supported by them?

options.text: Fewer Brennan students are studying abroad this year than in some previous year.
options.why: This year's number is the highest ever, so this contradicts the stimulus.

options.text: This year, more than twice as many Brennan students were eligible to study abroad as actually did so.
options.why: Everyone who went was eligible, and fewer than half of the eligible went, so eligible students outnumber those who went by more than two to one.

options.text: Most Brennan students who complete two years of a foreign language do not want to study abroad.
options.why: Choosing not to go isn't the same as not wanting to. Cost or scheduling could explain it.

options.text: Brennan College recently increased its foreign language requirement.
options.why: Nothing in the stimulus mentions a change in the requirement.

options.text: More Brennan students were eligible to study abroad this year than in any previous year.
options.why: Tempting, but a past year could have had more eligible students and a lower participation rate.

items.tldr: All who went were eligible, and under half of the eligible went, so eligible students outnumber them more than two to one.

steps.label: Task
steps.body: Most strongly supported. Find what the facts prove, not what's merely likely.

steps.label: Combine
steps.body: Students abroad ⊆ eligible students, and abroad < ½ × eligible. So eligible > 2 × abroad.

steps.label: Trap
steps.body: A record number abroad doesn't mean a record number eligible. Counts and rates can move independently.

items.takeaway: Proportions constrain counts. "Fewer than half went" means non-goers outnumber goers, but a record count of goers doesn't imply a record pool.

items.stimulus: Some economists argue that raising the minimum wage always reduces employment. But this view cannot be right. Several regions that raised their minimum wage last year saw employment grow, and economists who study those regions found no evidence that employment would have grown faster without the increase.
items.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the conclusion drawn in the argument?

options.text: Economists who study regional employment are more reliable than other economists.
options.why: The argument never compares the reliability of economists.

options.text: Raising the minimum wage never reduces employment.
options.why: The author denies "always reduces," which is not the same as claiming "never reduces."

options.text: It is not the case that raising the minimum wage always reduces employment.
options.why: That's the claim "this view cannot be right," spelled out. Everything after it is evidence for it.

options.text: Employment grew last year in several regions that raised their minimum wage.
options.why: This is evidence the author offers, not what the evidence is meant to show.

options.text: Raising the minimum wage tends to increase employment.
options.why: The author only shows that raises don't always cut jobs, not that they usually add them.

items.tldr: The conclusion is the rejection itself: raising the minimum wage doesn't always reduce employment.

steps.label: Find
steps.body: "But this view cannot be right" is the author's position. Translate "this view" back into words.

steps.label: Check
steps.body: The regional data support it, so they're premises, not the conclusion.

steps.label: Calibrate
steps.body: Denying "always" isn't asserting "never." Keep the answer exactly that strong.

items.takeaway: When an author rejects someone else's view, the rejection is usually the main conclusion. Match its strength exactly.

items.stimulus: Museum director: Some board members want to charge admission to pay for new exhibits. But an admission fee would discourage the students and low-income families our charter obliges us to serve. Admittedly, a fee would raise substantial revenue. Still, we should fund the exhibits through private donations instead.
items.prompt: The claim that a fee would raise substantial revenue plays which one of the following roles in the director's argument?

options.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument.
options.why: The conclusion is that the museum should seek private donations instead.

options.text: It is an intermediate conclusion supported by the claim about the museum's charter.
options.why: The charter point supports the main conclusion, not the revenue claim.

options.text: It is a claim that the director tries to show is false.
options.why: The director accepts the claim. She just thinks other factors outweigh it.

options.text: It is offered as direct support for the argument's conclusion.
options.why: Revenue from a fee argues for the fee, not for seeking donations instead.

options.text: It is a consideration the director concedes that might seem to count against the conclusion.
options.why: "Admittedly" signals a concession: revenue is a point in the fee's favor that the director acknowledges.

items.tldr: "Admittedly" marks a concession: revenue counts against the conclusion, and the director grants it.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: Conclusion: fund exhibits through donations. Support: a fee would deter those the charter requires serving.

steps.label: Role
steps.body: The revenue claim points the other way, and the director grants it before rejecting the fee anyway.

items.takeaway: Concession signals ("admittedly," "granted," "although") mark points the author accepts but argues past.

items.stimulus: After the town of Pell installed brighter streetlights on its main roads, the number of nighttime traffic accidents on those roads increased, even though the brighter lights make it easier for drivers to see.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?

options.text: Most residents of Pell approved of the decision to install the new lights.
options.why: Residents' approval doesn't explain the accident numbers.

options.text: The brighter streetlights cost more to operate than the old ones did.
options.why: Operating cost has nothing to do with the number of accidents.

options.text: Several other towns that installed brighter streetlights saw nighttime accidents decrease.
options.why: That makes Pell's increase more surprising, not less.

options.text: Brighter streetlights also make it easier for pedestrians to see oncoming cars.
options.why: Another safety benefit makes the rise in accidents even more puzzling.

options.text: After the new lights were installed, many drivers who had avoided Pell's main roads at night began using them, greatly increasing nighttime traffic.
options.why: More cars on the road can mean more accidents in total, even if each driver sees better.

items.tldr: Better visibility can coexist with more accidents if many more people drive at night.

steps.label: Facts
steps.body: Brighter lights improve visibility, yet nighttime accidents rose.

steps.label: Prephrase
steps.body: Something else changed: more drivers, faster driving, or more risk-taking.

steps.label: Check
steps.body: The right answer keeps both facts true. More traffic does that: the rate per driver can fall while the total rises.

items.takeaway: Resolve a paradox by explaining how both facts hold. Totals can rise while per-person rates fall.

items.stimulus: Columnist: The city should not adopt the proposed downtown parking rules. Although the rules would ease traffic congestion, they would make it much harder for disabled residents to reach the medical offices located downtown.
items.prompt: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the columnist's reasoning?

options.text: A city should adopt any policy that would ease congestion downtown.
options.why: This supports adopting the rules, the opposite of the columnist's conclusion.

options.text: No policy should be adopted unless every resident supports it.
options.why: The columnist's argument is about access to medical care, not unanimous support.

options.text: A policy that would significantly impede disabled residents' access to medical care should not be adopted, even if it has other benefits.
options.why: It matches the evidence (harder access to medical offices) to the conclusion (don't adopt), even granting the congestion benefit.

options.text: Congestion downtown is a more serious problem than limited access to medical offices.
options.why: This would favor adopting the rules.

options.text: Cities should provide more parking near medical offices than near other businesses.
options.why: This doesn't address whether these particular rules should be rejected.

items.tldr: The principle has to say that harming disabled residents' access to care outweighs the congestion benefit.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: Benefit: less congestion. Cost: disabled residents lose access to care. Conclusion: don't adopt.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: The principle should rank that cost above that benefit, specifically and without overreaching.

items.takeaway: A justifying principle connects this argument's evidence to its conclusion, and doesn't go further.

items.stimulus: If Lena takes the overnight train, she will arrive before the conference begins. If she arrives before the conference begins, she will give the opening talk. But Lena will not give the opening talk. So Lena will not take the overnight train.
items.prompt: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?

options.text: If the bakery does not open early, it will not sell out by noon. The bakery will not open early. So the owner will not bake a second batch.
options.why: Its premises and conclusion don't line up with the original's chain-and-denial pattern.

options.text: If the bakery opens early, it will sell out by noon, and if it sells out by noon, the owner will bake a second batch. So if the owner bakes a second batch, the bakery opened early.
options.why: It reverses the chain's direction instead of denying its end.

options.text: If the bakery opens early, it will sell out of bread by noon. If it sells out by noon, the owner will bake a second batch. The owner will not bake a second batch. So the bakery will not open early.
options.why: Same chain (P → Q, Q → R), same denial of the last link (not R), same valid conclusion (not P).

options.text: The bakery will open early only if it sells out by noon. The bakery will sell out by noon. So the bakery will open early.
options.why: "Only if" introduces a necessary condition. Meeting it doesn't guarantee the bakery opens early.

options.text: If the bakery opens early, it will sell out of bread by noon. The bakery will sell out of bread by noon. So the bakery will open early.
options.why: This affirms the result to conclude the condition, which is invalid. The original is valid.

items.tldr: Deny the chain's end to deny its start: P→Q→R, not R, so not P. Only one bakery argument copies that exactly.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: Overnight train → arrive early → opening talk. Not opening talk. So not overnight train.

steps.label: Abstract
steps.body: P → Q, Q → R, not R, therefore not P. That's a valid chained contrapositive.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: Find the same links and the same move. Ignore the topic entirely.

items.takeaway: Parallel questions test structure. Translate the stimulus into letters, then find the answer with the same letters.

items.stimulus: Every licensed pilot has passed a vision test. Marco has passed a vision test. So Marco must be a licensed pilot.
items.prompt: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

options.text: Some first-aid instructors are certified lifeguards. Priya is a first-aid instructor. So Priya is a certified lifeguard.
options.why: Flawed, but it misuses "some," a different error from the original's reversal.

options.text: Every certified lifeguard has completed a first-aid course. Priya is a certified lifeguard. So Priya has completed a first-aid course.
options.why: This applies the rule correctly. It's valid.

options.text: Most certified lifeguards are strong swimmers. Priya is a certified lifeguard. So Priya is probably a strong swimmer.
options.why: A cautious probabilistic inference, not the reversal in the original.

options.text: Every certified lifeguard has completed a first-aid course. Priya has not completed a first-aid course. So Priya is not a certified lifeguard.
options.why: This is the valid contrapositive, so there's no flaw to match.

options.text: Every certified lifeguard has completed a first-aid course. Priya has completed a first-aid course. So Priya must be a certified lifeguard.
options.why: Same flaw: meeting a requirement is treated as proof of belonging to the group.
