items.tldr: The original treats a requirement (passing a vision test) as a guarantee. Only the argument that treats a first-aid course as proof of being a lifeguard makes the same mistake.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: Pilot → passed test. Marco passed the test. So Marco is a pilot.

steps.label: Name the flaw
steps.body: It reverses the conditional, treating a necessary condition as sufficient.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: Find the answer with the same reversal. Valid arguments can't match a flawed one.

items.takeaway: In parallel flaw questions, name the flaw first, then eliminate every answer that's valid or flawed in a different way.

items.stimulus:
Amara: The city's new bike lanes have made downtown streets safer. Serious collisions there have dropped by a third since the lanes opened.
Desmond: The drop in collisions isn't due to the bike lanes. The city lowered the downtown speed limit at the same time, and slower traffic alone would explain the decline.
items.prompt: Amara and Desmond disagree over whether

options.text: the bike lanes are responsible for the decline in serious collisions downtown
options.why: Amara credits the bike lanes; Desmond credits the lower speed limit instead.

options.text: the downtown speed limit should be lowered further
options.why: Neither speaker says anything about lowering it further.

options.text: serious collisions downtown have declined since the bike lanes opened
options.why: Desmond accepts the decline. He disputes its cause.

options.text: the city should build more bike lanes
options.why: Neither speaker makes a recommendation.

options.text: bike lanes make streets safer in every city
options.why: Both speakers talk only about this city's downtown.

items.tldr: They agree collisions fell; they disagree about whether the bike lanes caused it.

steps.label: Amara
steps.body: Collisions fell, and the bike lanes made the streets safer.

steps.label: Desmond
steps.body: Collisions fell, but the lower speed limit, not the lanes, explains it.

steps.label: Test
steps.body: The answer must be something both address and disagree on. Only the cause qualifies.

items.takeaway: For disagreement questions, check each answer against both speakers. Each must have a view, and the views must conflict.

items.stimulus: Critic: The mayor claims that no public project in this city has ever been finished on time. But the Harbor Bridge, a public project, opened two months ahead of schedule.
items.prompt: The critic responds to the mayor's claim by

options.text: showing that the mayor's claim contradicts itself
options.why: The claim is contradicted by a fact, not by itself.

options.text: offering a counterexample to a general claim
options.why: One project finished early is enough to refute "no public project has ever been on time."

options.text: arguing that most public projects in the city are finished on time
options.why: The critic cites one project. That says nothing about most projects.

options.text: questioning the mayor's motives for making the claim
options.why: The critic never mentions the mayor's motives.

options.text: providing evidence that the Harbor Bridge cost less than projected
options.why: Cost is never mentioned. The point is the schedule.

items.tldr: A single on-time project refutes "no project has ever been on time." That's a counterexample.

steps.label: Claim
steps.body: Mayor: no public project here has ever been finished on time.

steps.label: Reply
steps.body: The critic names one public project that was early.

steps.label: Method
steps.body: One counterexample defeats a universal claim.

items.takeaway: "Never" and "always" claims fall to a single counterexample, but one example doesn't prove the opposite generalization.

items.stimulus: Since the town of Brook Falls began offering free swimming lessons for children, drowning incidents involving children there have fallen sharply. So the free lessons have made children in Brook Falls safer around water.
items.prompt: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the argument?

options.text: How many adults in Brook Falls know how to swim
options.why: The argument is about children; adult swimming ability doesn't test the causal claim.

options.text: Whether Brook Falls began posting lifeguards at its public beaches when the lessons began
options.why: If yes, lifeguards are a rival cause and the argument weakens. If no, a major alternative is ruled out and it strengthens.

options.text: Whether other towns near Brook Falls offer swimming lessons for adults
options.why: Adult lessons in other towns don't bear on what caused Brook Falls' decline.

options.text: Whether most children in Brook Falls enjoy swimming
options.why: Enjoyment doesn't affect whether the lessons caused the drop in drownings.

options.text: Whether drowning incidents are more common in summer than in winter
options.why: Seasonal patterns apply before and after the lessons alike.

items.tldr: Knowing whether lifeguards arrived at the same time would either rule out or reveal a rival cause.

steps.label: Core
steps.body: Drownings fell after free lessons began, so the lessons made children safer.

steps.label: Gap
steps.body: Something else that changed at the same time could explain the drop.

steps.label: Test
steps.body: The right question has an answer that matters either way. Lifeguards does.

items.takeaway: An evaluate answer is a question whose answer would strengthen the argument one way and weaken it the other.

items.stimulus: Every member of the debate team takes a logic course. No one who takes a logic course is exempt from the writing requirement. Carla is exempt from the writing requirement.
items.prompt: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

options.text: Carla does not take any courses.
options.why: We only know she doesn't take a logic course.

options.text: Some members of the debate team are exempt from the writing requirement.
options.why: Every debate member takes logic, and no logic student is exempt.

options.text: Carla is not a member of the debate team.
options.why: Exempt → no logic course → not on the debate team (two contrapositives chained).

options.text: Carla takes a logic course but is not on the debate team.
options.why: Logic students aren't exempt, and Carla is, so she can't take logic.

options.text: Everyone who takes a logic course is a member of the debate team.
options.why: That reverses "debate team → logic course."

items.tldr: Exempt → no logic course → not on the debate team.

steps.label: Chain
steps.body: Debate → logic → not exempt.

steps.label: Contrapositive
steps.body: Exempt → not logic → not debate.

steps.label: Apply
steps.body: Carla is exempt, so she isn't on the debate team.

items.takeaway: Chain the conditionals, then run the contrapositive backward from the fact you're given.

items.stimulus: Dr. Reyes argues that the new zoning plan will raise housing costs. But Dr. Reyes owns several rental properties in the city, so her argument should be dismissed.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

options.text: fails to explain why the zoning plan was proposed
options.why: The plan's origins aren't relevant to the flaw.

options.text: relies on the opinion of a single expert
options.why: It doesn't rely on her opinion; it dismisses it.

options.text: assumes that housing costs will rise regardless of the zoning plan
options.why: The argument makes no prediction about housing costs.

options.text: confuses a cause of rising housing costs with an effect of them
options.why: No causal claim is made.

options.text: rejects an argument because of a fact about the person making it rather than the argument's merits
options.why: Owning rentals might give her a motive, but it says nothing about whether she's right.

items.tldr: It dismisses her argument because of who she is, not what she argues.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: Conclusion: dismiss Dr. Reyes's argument. Reason: she owns rental properties.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.body: A possible bias doesn't make an argument wrong. The argument never addresses her evidence.

items.takeaway: Attacking the arguer (ad hominem) is a flaw. Motives can raise suspicion but can't refute reasoning.

items.stimulus: A survey of members of the Riverside Cycling Club found that 85 percent support adding bike lanes to Main Street. So most residents of Riverside support adding bike lanes to Main Street.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: Members of the Riverside Cycling Club ride bicycles far more often than most Riverside residents do.
options.why: The sample differs from residents in exactly the way that shapes views on bike lanes, so it isn't representative.

options.text: The survey was conducted by the club's own volunteers.
options.why: It hints at bias but doesn't show the results misrepresent residents.

options.text: Bike lanes have been added to streets in several nearby towns.
options.why: Other towns don't tell us what Riverside residents think.

options.text: Some club members do not live on Main Street.
options.why: The conclusion is about Riverside residents, not Main Street residents.

options.text: Most club members who support the bike lanes also support wider sidewalks.
options.why: Views on sidewalks don't affect whether the sample represents residents.

items.tldr: Cyclists aren't typical residents, so a cycling club can't speak for the town on bike lanes.

steps.label: Core
steps.body: Club members support bike lanes, so most residents do.

steps.label: Gap
steps.body: It assumes club members represent all residents.

steps.label: Attack
steps.body: Show the sample differs in a way that matters. Frequent cyclists do.

items.takeaway: Survey arguments fall when the sample differs from the population in a way that bears on the question asked.

items.stimulus: Library director: Our new self-checkout kiosks will reduce the time patrons wait in line. After all, patrons who use the kiosks won't need to wait for a staff member to check out their books.
items.prompt: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the director's argument?

options.text: At least some patrons will use the self-checkout kiosks rather than wait for a staff member.
options.why: Negate it and no one uses the kiosks, so lines can't get shorter.

options.text: Staff members will be reassigned to other tasks once the kiosks are installed.
options.why: The argument doesn't need this, and if true it might lengthen lines.

options.text: The kiosks cost less to operate than hiring more staff would.
options.why: Cost has nothing to do with waiting time.

options.text: Every patron who uses the kiosks will finish checking out in under a minute.
options.why: Kiosks can help without every checkout being that fast.

options.text: Most patrons prefer self-checkout to checking out with a staff member.
options.why: Even a minority using the kiosks could shorten lines. "Most" isn't required.

items.tldr: If nobody uses the kiosks, waiting time can't fall, so the argument needs some to use them.

steps.label: Core
steps.body: Kiosk users skip the staff line, so waiting time will fall.

steps.label: Gap
steps.body: That only works if someone actually uses the kiosks.

steps.label: Check
steps.body: Negate the right answer ("no patrons use them") and the argument collapses.

items.takeaway: Necessary assumptions are often modest ("at least some"). Answers with "most" or "every" usually ask for more than the argument needs.

items.stimulus: After the Greenvale school district began serving breakfast to all students at no cost, the district's average attendance rose by four percentage points. The superintendent concludes that the free breakfast program improved attendance.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the superintendent's argument?

options.text: Attendance in neighboring districts that did not offer free breakfast stayed the same over the same period.
options.why: It rules out a regional trend that would have raised attendance anyway.

options.text: Some students who eat the free breakfast still miss school occasionally.
options.why: The claim is about average attendance; some absences are expected either way.

options.text: The free breakfast program has cost the district more than expected.
options.why: Cost doesn't bear on whether breakfast improved attendance.

options.text: Greenvale also began a new attendance-reward program that year.
options.why: That's a rival cause, so it weakens the argument.

options.text: Many Greenvale students had already been eating breakfast at home before the program began.
options.why: If many already ate breakfast, the program changed less, which undercuts it.

items.tldr: If similar districts without free breakfast saw no change, the breakfast is the likelier cause.

steps.label: Core
steps.body: Free breakfast began, then attendance rose, so breakfast raised attendance.

steps.label: Alternatives
steps.body: A regional trend or another new program could explain the rise.

steps.label: Fix
steps.body: A comparison group without the program, and without the rise, rules out a trend.

items.takeaway: A comparison group that didn't get the change, and didn't improve, is one of the strongest strengtheners for a causal claim.

items.stimulus: The share of Fairport's budget spent on parks fell from 6 percent last year to 5 percent this year. Clearly, Fairport is spending less money on its parks than it did last year.
items.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because it

options.text: assumes that parks are the most important part of the budget
options.why: The argument says nothing about importance.

options.text: confuses the number of parks with the amount spent on them
options.why: The number of parks is never mentioned.

options.text: takes for granted that spending on parks should never decrease
options.why: No such value judgment appears.

options.text: overlooks the possibility that Fairport's total budget grew enough that 5 percent of it is more money than 6 percent of last year's budget
options.why: A smaller share of a bigger budget can still be more money.

options.text: compares figures from only two years
options.why: Comparing two years is fine. The problem is mixing shares with amounts.

items.tldr: A smaller percentage of a larger budget can be more dollars.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: The parks' share of the budget fell from 6% to 5%.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Parks are getting less money.

steps.label: Gap
steps.body: It ignores the size of the total. Percentages alone can't show amounts.

items.takeaway: When evidence is a percentage and the conclusion is an amount (or the reverse), check whether the total changed.

items.stimulus: A hospital installed hand-sanitizer stations outside every patient room, and staff used them far more often than they had used the old sinks. Yet the number of reported hospital-acquired infections rose over the following year.
items.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the apparent discrepancy?

options.text: Sanitizer kills many of the germs that cause hospital-acquired infections.
options.why: That makes a rise in infections more surprising, not less.

options.text: The number of patients the hospital treated stayed the same.
options.why: It rules out patient volume as an explanation, so the puzzle remains.

options.text: Staff at many other hospitals also use sanitizer stations.
options.why: Other hospitals don't explain this hospital's numbers.

options.text: Hand sanitizer is less expensive than soap and water.
options.why: Cost doesn't explain the rise in reported infections.

options.text: When the stations were installed, the hospital began testing every patient for infections, so many infections that once went undetected were now reported.
options.why: Reported infections can rise even if actual infections fell, because more are being found.

items.tldr: Wider testing made more infections visible, so reported numbers rose despite better hygiene.

steps.label: Facts
steps.body: Hand hygiene improved, yet reported infections rose.

steps.label: Notice
steps.body: The stimulus says "reported." Reporting can change even if reality doesn't.

steps.label: Resolve
steps.body: More testing finds more cases, which reconciles both facts.

items.takeaway: Watch for "reported" or "recorded" in paradoxes. A change in measurement can explain a surprising rise.

items.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

options.text: The evidentiary justification is the best explanation of the doctrine as courts apply it.
options.why: P3 argues that this justification can't explain the hostility requirement.

options.text: The traditional justifications for adverse possession do not fully account for how the doctrine is applied, which is better explained by the law's concern for a possessor's reliance on the land.
options.why: This covers the critique of both traditional justifications (P3) and the author's alternative (P4).

options.text: The doctrine of adverse possession should be abolished because it rewards trespass.
options.why: That objection is reported in P1; the author ends up explaining the doctrine, not rejecting it.

options.text: Property is nothing more than a practical connection between people and places.
options.why: The author says property is not only abstract rights but also a practical connection.

options.text: Courts apply adverse possession inconsistently because they misunderstand its purpose.
options.why: The author faults the traditional justifications, not the courts.

items.tldr: Both traditional justifications fall short; protecting the possessor's reliance explains the doctrine better.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: P1 doctrine and objection. P2 two justifications. P3 both fall short. P4 the reliance account.

steps.label: Main point
steps.body: The passage's own claim is in P3 and P4 together.

items.takeaway: The main point usually combines what the author rejects with what the author proposes instead.

items.prompt: The author mentions a tenant who stays on after a lease expires primarily in order to

options.text: suggest that leases are poor evidence of who owns a piece of land
options.why: The point concerns evidence of occupation, not the value of leases.

options.text: illustrate a case in which a court would award title to the possessor
options.why: The tenant has permission, so the possession isn't hostile and title wouldn't pass.

options.text: argue that tenants should be able to acquire title by adverse possession
options.why: The author never makes that proposal.

options.text: show that the evidentiary justification cannot explain why possession must be hostile
options.why: Such a tenant gives equally good evidence of long occupation, yet can't gain title because the possession isn't hostile.

options.text: support the justification based on the owner's neglect
options.why: The tenant example targets the evidentiary justification, and P3 criticizes both.

items.tldr: The tenant shows long occupation without hostility, which the evidence rationale can't explain.

steps.label: Locate
steps.body: "If the concern were only evidence, the law would not require that the possession be hostile..."

steps.label: Role
steps.body: The tenant is the counterexample that proves the point.

items.takeaway: A hypothetical case right after "if the concern were only..." is usually a counterexample.

items.prompt: According to the passage, which one of the following is a requirement for acquiring title by adverse possession?

options.text: A court must approve the occupation before it begins.
options.why: No such requirement appears in the passage.

options.text: The occupier must have entered the land with the owner's permission.
options.why: Possession must be hostile, meaning without the owner's permission.

options.text: The occupier must have surveyed the boundaries of the land.
options.why: Surveys appear only in the fence example.

options.text: The occupation must be continuous for a period set by statute.
options.why: P1 lists open, continuous, exclusive and hostile possession for a statutory period.

options.text: The owner must have received written notice of the occupation.
options.why: Notice to the owner isn't listed as a requirement.

items.tldr: Open, continuous, exclusive, hostile, for the statutory period.

steps.label: Locate
steps.body: The first sentence of P1 lists the requirements.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: Only continuity for the statutory period appears there.

items.takeaway: For detail questions, go back to the line. Don't answer from memory.

items.prompt: The justification based on the owner's conduct (paragraph 2) would most clearly support awarding title to the possessor in which one of the following cases?

options.text: An owner who lives next door knowingly lets a stranger farm her field openly for fifteen years without objecting.
options.why: Knowingly ignoring an open occupation for over a decade is exactly the neglect this justification relies on.

options.text: A person occupies vacant land openly for two years.
options.why: Two years falls well short of the decade or more the justification describes.

options.text: A tenant stays on with the owner's permission after a lease expires.
options.why: Permissive possession isn't hostile, and the owner isn't neglecting anything.

options.text: An owner visits her land every year and objects each time to the occupier's presence.
options.why: That owner is asserting her interest, not abandoning it.

options.text: An owner has no reason to suspect that a neighbor's fence sits a few feet over their unsurveyed boundary.
options.why: The author uses this case to show where the neglect justification fails.

items.tldr: The neglect rationale fits an owner who knowingly does nothing for years.

steps.label: The rationale
steps.body: An owner who ignores an open occupation for a decade or more has effectively abandoned the land.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: Knowledge, inaction and a long period all appear only in the neighbor's case.

items.takeaway: Apply a view by checking each of its conditions against the case.

items.prompt: The author's attitude toward the reliance account (paragraph 4) can most accurately be described as

options.text: skeptical of its usefulness
options.why: The author offers it as the better explanation.

options.text: favorable, while acknowledging that it does not answer every objection to the doctrine
options.why: The author calls it "more satisfying" but adds that it "does not make the doctrine immune from criticism."

options.text: unreservedly enthusiastic
options.why: The author explicitly notes the account's limits.

options.text: neutral, since the author takes no position on the doctrine
options.why: The author clearly prefers this account to the traditional ones.

options.text: grudging, accepting it only because the alternatives fail
options.why: The author praises what it recognizes about property, which is more than grudging acceptance.

items.tldr: Favorable, with a stated limit.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: "A more satisfying account..." and "does not make the doctrine immune from criticism."

steps.label: Attitude
steps.body: Positive, with a qualification.

items.takeaway: A qualifier ("does not make it immune") rules out extreme attitude answers.

items.prompt: The author would most likely agree with which one of the following statements?

options.text: The evidentiary justification has nothing to do with the doctrine.
options.why: The author says it doesn't fully explain the doctrine, not that it's irrelevant.

options.text: Owners should be legally required to survey their boundaries regularly.
options.why: The author never proposes any duty to survey.

options.text: Lost deeds are usually evidence of fraud.
options.why: Lost deeds come up only as an evidentiary problem.

options.text: An adequate account of adverse possession should explain why the doctrine focuses on what the possessor has done.
options.why: The author praises the reliance account precisely because it explains that focus.

options.text: Adverse possession is rarely invoked in modern courts.
options.why: The passage says nothing about how often the doctrine is used.

items.tldr: The author wants the account to explain the doctrine's focus on the possessor.

steps.label: Find the line
steps.body: The reliance account "explains why the law asks what the possessor has done."

steps.label: Infer
steps.body: The author treats explaining that focus as a mark of a good account.

items.takeaway: What the author praises an account for doing tells you what the author values.

items.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

options.text: Two competing legal doctrines are compared, and one of them is endorsed.
options.why: Only one doctrine is discussed; the comparison is between justifications for it.

options.text: A doctrine is criticized, then defended, and finally rejected.
options.why: The passage ends by explaining the doctrine, not rejecting it.

options.text: A problem is described and several solutions are rejected, with no alternative offered.
options.why: The author does offer an alternative account.

options.text: A legal doctrine is described and a common objection noted; two traditional justifications are presented and shown to be incomplete; an alternative justification is proposed.
options.why: That matches P1, P2, P3 and P4 in order.

options.text: The history of a doctrine is traced, followed by predictions about its future.
options.why: The passage makes no historical survey or predictions.

items.tldr: Doctrine and objection, two justifications, their flaws, a better account.

steps.label: Label each paragraph
steps.body: P1 describe and object. P2 justify. P3 critique. P4 propose.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: Pick the answer whose sequence matches every step.

items.takeaway: For organization questions, label each paragraph's job first, then match the sequence.

items.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

options.text: Wegener's hypothesis was rejected mainly because he was not a geologist.
options.why: The author grants that this played some role but says it obscures the substantive objection.

options.text: Scientific establishments are generally unwilling to accept new ideas.
options.why: The author resists exactly this reading of the episode.

options.text: Wegener's evidence was too weak to support the idea of continental drift.
options.why: The author calls his evidence impressive; the missing piece was a mechanism.

options.text: Plate tectonics replaced continental drift after drift was disproved.
options.why: Plate tectonics vindicated drift by supplying its mechanism.

options.text: The long rejection of Wegener's hypothesis reflected a reasonable demand for a mechanism, a demand later met by evidence of seafloor spreading.
options.why: The passage argues the rejection was reasonable (P2–P3) and explains how the mechanism arrived (P4).

items.tldr: Geologists reasonably wanted a mechanism, and seafloor spreading supplied it.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: P1 strong evidence, long rejection. P2 the popular story versus the real objection. P3 the objection was reasonable. P4 the mechanism arrives.

steps.label: Main point
steps.body: Reasonable rejection, then vindication once a mechanism appeared.

items.takeaway: When an author corrects a popular story, the correction is usually the main point.

items.prompt: The author mentions that Wegener was a meteorologist primarily in order to

options.text: argue that outsiders often make important scientific discoveries
options.why: No such general claim is made.

options.text: suggest that Wegener's evidence came mainly from studies of weather
options.why: His evidence came from coastlines, fossils, rocks and glacial traces.

options.text: explain why the mechanisms Wegener proposed were too weak
options.why: The passage attributes their weakness to physics, not to his training.

options.text: show that the critics' objection to his mechanism was unfair
options.why: The author calls that objection reasonable.

options.text: concede that part of the popular account of his rejection is accurate
options.why: It follows "That story contains some truth" and explains why some critics dismissed him as an outsider.

items.tldr: His outsider status is the true part of the "conservatism" story.

steps.label: Context
steps.body: "That story contains some truth. Wegener was a meteorologist, not a geologist..."

steps.label: Role
steps.body: A concession before the "But" that introduces the real objection.

items.takeaway: Details sandwiched between "contains some truth" and "But" are concessions.

items.prompt: The author's attitude toward the geologists who rejected Wegener's hypothesis is best described as

options.text: admiring of their foresight in anticipating plate tectonics
options.why: The author never credits them with anticipating the later theory.

options.text: indifferent to whether their rejection was justified
options.why: The author argues at length that it was justified.

options.text: largely sympathetic, regarding their main objection as reasonable
options.why: The author says the objection "was reasonable" and that they weren't refusing to look at the evidence.

options.text: critical of their refusal to examine Wegener's evidence
options.why: The author says they were not refusing to look at the evidence.

options.text: contemptuous of their conservatism
options.why: The author pushes back against the conservatism story.

items.tldr: Sympathetic, since their demand for a mechanism was reasonable.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: "The objection was reasonable."

steps.label: Attitude
steps.body: The author defends the skeptics against the popular story.

items.takeaway: Watch for the author defending a group that a popular story blames.

items.prompt: According to the passage, which one of the following helped show that new seafloor forms at mid-ocean ridges?

options.text: calculations of forces arising from Earth's rotation
options.why: Those calculations showed that Wegener's proposed mechanism was too weak.

options.text: the matching coastlines of South America and Africa
options.why: That was Wegener's evidence for drift, not for seafloor spreading.

options.text: symmetrical stripes of rock recording reversals of Earth's magnetic field
options.why: P4 says these stripes, on either side of the ridges, indicated that new seafloor forms and spreads.

options.text: fossils of the same reptiles on continents separated by oceans
options.why: Also Wegener's evidence, gathered long before.

options.text: traces of ancient glaciers that match across the Atlantic
options.why: Another part of Wegener's original evidence.

items.tldr: The magnetic stripes beside the ridges showed seafloor spreading.

steps.label: Locate
steps.body: P4 lists mid-ocean ridges and magnetic stripes.

steps.label: Separate the evidence
steps.body: Wegener's evidence (P1) is different from the seafloor evidence (P4).

items.takeaway: Keep track of which evidence supports which claim; RC traps swap them.

items.prompt: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following statements?

options.text: The continents move through the solid ocean floor, as Wegener believed.
options.why: The continents ride along with the seafloor on plates.

options.text: Wegener lived to see his hypothesis accepted by most geologists.
options.why: The passage never says when Wegener died or what he saw.

options.text: The evidence Wegener assembled did not by itself change geologists' minds; a mechanism made it persuasive.
options.why: P4 says the impasse was broken by a different kind of evidence, after which "the old evidence... was suddenly persuasive."

options.text: Most of Wegener's evidence was later found to be mistaken.
options.why: His old evidence became persuasive once the mechanism was found.

options.text: Geologists in the 1950s had never heard of Wegener's hypothesis.
options.why: Nothing suggests his hypothesis was unknown.

items.tldr: The same evidence persuaded once a mechanism existed.

steps.label: Find the line
steps.body: "With a mechanism in hand, the old evidence for drift was suddenly persuasive."

steps.label: Infer
steps.body: The evidence alone hadn't been enough.

items.takeaway: Look for the sentence that explains a change; the inference usually paraphrases it.

items.prompt: Which one of the following is most analogous to the history of Wegener's hypothesis as the author describes it?

options.text: A diagnosis that fits all of a patient's symptoms is doubted because no known disease process could produce them together, until a new test reveals one.
options.why: Strong fit to the evidence, doubt over the missing mechanism, then acceptance once the mechanism appears.

options.text: Two rival theories explain the same evidence equally well, and scientists remain divided.
options.why: The episode ended with a clear resolution.

options.text: A theory is rejected after its supporting evidence is found to be fabricated.
options.why: Wegener's evidence was sound; the problem was a missing mechanism.

options.text: A theory with little supporting evidence is accepted because its mechanism is plausible.
options.why: Wegener had plenty of evidence but no plausible mechanism, the reverse.

options.text: A theory is accepted quickly because its author is famous, and is later abandoned.
options.why: Wegener's theory was rejected for decades, not accepted quickly.

items.tldr: Good evidence, no mechanism, then a mechanism and acceptance.

steps.label: Abstract the story
steps.body: Evidence fits; process seems impossible; new findings supply the process; acceptance follows.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: Only the diagnosis case has all four stages.

items.takeaway: Strip the passage's story to its stages, then match an answer stage by stage.

items.prompt: The author would be most likely to endorse which one of the following principles?

options.text: Hypotheses proposed by scientists outside a field deserve less scrutiny than others.
options.why: The author never says outsiders deserve different treatment.

options.text: Scientists should accept whichever hypothesis fits the most observations, whatever its mechanism.
options.why: The author defends withholding assent from a hypothesis that fit many observations but lacked a mechanism.

options.text: Fossil evidence is more reliable than geological evidence.
options.why: The passage doesn't rank kinds of evidence.

options.text: An account of what happened should be compatible with some account of how it could have happened.
options.why: The author describes exactly this insistence as reasonable in P3.

options.text: A hypothesis should be rejected if its author was trained in a different field.
options.why: The author treats dismissal of Wegener as an outsider as the weakest part of the story.

items.tldr: The author endorses demanding a possible "how" for any "what."

steps.label: Find the line
steps.body: Geologists insisted "an account of what happened must be compatible with an account of how it could happen."

steps.label: Author's stance
steps.body: The author calls that objection reasonable.

items.takeaway: Principles the author attributes to a group and then praises are principles the author endorses.

items.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

options.text: Homer's repetitions are a flaw that modern readers are right to criticize.
options.why: The passage argues the repetitions reflect an art with different demands.

options.text: Homer's poems were composed entirely in performance and were never written down.
options.why: P4 notes that some scholars think the poems were written down, perhaps with the poet's help.

options.text: Parry's theory has been refuted by evidence of large-scale design in the poems.
options.why: The author says the theory left questions open but changed the terms of the debate.

options.text: Parry's account of Homer's epithets as tools of oral composition, supported by fieldwork with oral singers, transformed how Homer's repetitions are understood, though some questions remain open.
options.why: It covers the theory (P1–P2), the fieldwork (P3) and its impact and limits (P4).

options.text: The Yugoslav singers memorized fixed texts of their songs.
options.why: They never performed a song in exactly the same words twice.

items.tldr: Parry recast Homer's repetitions as oral tools, a view that transformed the field despite open questions.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: P1 puzzle and Parry's idea. P2 epithets fit the meter. P3 fieldwork. P4 impact and limits.

steps.label: Main point
steps.body: The theory's argument and its transforming effect, with limits.

items.takeaway: Include the author's qualifications in the main point when the passage stresses them.

items.prompt: According to the passage, Parry argued that a system of fixed epithets would be

options.text: indispensable to a poet composing aloud at speed before an audience
options.why: P2 says such a system would be "indispensable to one composing aloud, at speed, before an audience."

options.text: unrelated to the meter of the line
options.why: Parry showed the epithets are tightly bound to meter.

options.text: a sign of a poet's lack of originality
options.why: That is the modern reader's view, which Parry challenged.

options.text: useful mainly to poets composing slowly in writing
options.why: Parry said it would be "of little use" to such poets.

options.text: an invention of Homer himself
options.why: Parry saw the formulas as part of a tradition, not one poet's invention.

items.tldr: The formulas are essential for composing aloud, fast.

steps.label: Locate
steps.body: The middle of P2.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: Indispensable for oral composition at speed.

items.takeaway: Distinguish the author's or scholar's view from the "modern readers'" view the passage sets against it.

items.prompt: The author describes singers who insisted that a song was the same "word for word" primarily in order to

options.text: prove that Homer's poems were never performed the same way twice
options.why: The Yugoslav evidence supports the theory but proves nothing directly about Homer's performances.

options.text: show that the singers understood a song's identity differently from the way a fixed text would define it
options.why: The paragraph concludes that for these singers a song's identity lay in its story and traditional elements.

options.text: suggest that the singers were deliberately misleading the researchers
options.why: The point is a different concept of sameness, not dishonesty.

options.text: criticize the methods Lord used to interview singers
options.why: No criticism of method appears.

options.text: cast doubt on the accuracy of Parry and Lord's recordings
options.why: The recordings are what reveal the variation.

items.tldr: The singers' "same song" meant the same story, not the same words.

steps.label: Locate
steps.body: The anecdote is followed by "For these performers, a song's identity lay in its story..."

steps.label: Role
steps.body: It illustrates a different idea of what makes a song the same.

items.takeaway: The sentence after an anecdote usually tells you what the anecdote is for.

items.prompt: The critics mentioned in paragraph 4 would be most likely to agree with which one of the following?

options.text: Homer was a literate poet who composed every line in writing.
options.why: Some scholars suggest an oral poet's composition was written down, not that Homer composed in writing.

options.text: The overall structure of the Iliad is difficult to explain as the product of performance alone.
options.why: They point to large-scale design "that seems hard to achieve in performance."

options.text: The Yugoslav songs are older than the Homeric poems.
options.why: The passage doesn't compare their ages.

options.text: Parry was wrong that Homer's epithets are bound to meter.
options.why: The critics question large-scale design, not the metrical analysis.

options.text: Repetition is always a flaw in poetry.
options.why: Nothing indicates the critics hold this view.

items.tldr: The critics doubt that performance alone could produce the poems' overall design.

steps.label: Find the line
steps.body: Large-scale design "seems hard to achieve in performance."

steps.label: Infer
steps.body: They doubt performance alone explains the poems' structure.

items.takeaway: Attribute to each group only what the passage says that group says.

items.prompt: The author's attitude toward Parry's theory can most accurately be described as

options.text: skeptical of its value overall
options.why: The author credits it with transforming the field.

options.text: uncritically accepting of every part of it
options.why: The author notes the critics' objections.

options.text: purely neutral, reporting the theory without evaluating it
options.why: "Insight" and "transformed" are evaluations.

options.text: admiring of its central insight, while acknowledging questions it left open
options.why: The author says it "transformed Homeric studies" and "changed the terms of the debate," though it "did not settle every question."

options.text: dismissive, because it ignores the poems' large-scale design
options.why: That is the critics' concern, and the author still credits the theory.

items.tldr: Admiring, with acknowledged limits.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: "Transformed," "insight," "though it did not settle every question."

steps.label: Attitude
steps.body: Positive and measured.

items.takeaway: Evaluative words such as "insight" and "transformed" reveal attitude even in an explanatory passage.

items.prompt: Which one of the following best exemplifies the kind of skill that the last sentence of the passage attributes to a poet in an oral tradition?

options.text: A scholar who catalogs every epithet used in Homer
options.why: Cataloging formulas isn't composing with them.

options.text: A composer who invents a new scale that no one has used before
options.why: That is originality, the value the passage contrasts with oral artistry.

options.text: A jazz musician improvising a solo by combining familiar phrases from the tradition in fresh and fitting ways
options.why: Skill lies in using traditional units well, in real time, before an audience.

options.text: An actor who memorizes a script and never departs from it
options.why: That treats the work as a fixed text, which the singers didn't.

options.text: A novelist who revises a manuscript for years to remove every phrase that sounds familiar
options.why: The oral poet's skill lies not in avoiding the traditional phrase.

items.tldr: Skill means using traditional pieces well in live performance.

steps.label: The skill
steps.body: "Not in avoiding the traditional phrase but in using it well."

steps.label: Match
steps.body: The improviser combines familiar phrases fittingly, on the spot.

items.takeaway: Analogy answers must match the defining feature, not just the subject area.

items.prompt: As used in the last sentence of the passage, "different demands" refers most directly to

options.text: the expectations of modern readers trained to prize originality
options.why: Those are the expectations of written literature that oral art is contrasted with.

options.text: the difficulty of creating large-scale design in performance
options.why: That is the critics' objection, not what the "different demands" of oral art refers to.

options.text: the challenge of translating the poems into other languages
options.why: Translation isn't discussed.

options.text: the need to compose quickly before an audience while keeping to the meter
options.why: Paragraph 2 explains that formulas serve a poet composing aloud, at speed, in meter.

options.text: the requirements of producing a fixed written text
options.why: The oral singers had no fixed text.

items.tldr: Oral composition demands speed, meter and an audience.

steps.label: Trace back
steps.body: The demands of oral art were laid out in P2.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: Composing aloud, at speed, within the meter.

items.takeaway: Phrases in a conclusion often point back to an earlier paragraph; find it.

items.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?

options.text: Passage A criticizes a policy that passage B defends.
options.why: A defends nudges; B criticizes them.

options.text: Passage B offers new evidence that undermines the findings described in passage A.
options.why: B accepts that defaults work; it questions how and for whom.

options.text: Both passages argue that defaults should be eliminated.
options.why: Both say some influence is unavoidable, and A endorses defaults.

options.text: Passage A presents evidence for a policy approach and argues for it; passage B raises concerns about that approach's transparency and its effects on some people.
options.why: A argues from the enrollment evidence to nudges; B questions their accountability and their fit for everyone.

options.text: Passage B summarizes passage A without evaluating it.
options.why: B clearly evaluates nudges.

items.tldr: A argues for nudges; B challenges their transparency and one-size-fits-all effects.

steps.label: A's stance
steps.body: Defaults work, influence is unavoidable, so set good defaults.

steps.label: B's stance
steps.body: Nudges escape scrutiny and don't suit everyone.

items.takeaway: Summarize each passage's stance in a few words before reading the answers.

items.prompt: The authors of both passages would most likely agree that

options.text: automatic enrollment leaves every worker better off
options.why: B says it can leave some workers worse off.

options.text: laws that require saving are preferable to defaults
options.why: B contrasts laws with defaults to make a point about visibility, but never says laws are better.

options.text: behavioral economics has little to teach policymakers
options.why: A draws a policy lesson from it, and B doesn't dispute the findings.

options.text: most people notice the defaults on enrollment forms
options.why: B says defaults work because most people never notice them.

options.text: institutions cannot avoid influencing the choices people make
options.why: A says institutions "cannot avoid influencing choices"; B calls such influence something "they cannot avoid."

items.tldr: Both say influence on choices is unavoidable.

steps.label: A
steps.body: "Institutions cannot avoid influencing choices."

steps.label: B
steps.body: "...whether institutions should influence choices, which they cannot avoid..."

items.takeaway: Agreement questions need a line from each passage. Find both before choosing.

items.prompt: The author of passage B would most likely respond to the claim in passage A that nudges "preserve freedom" by arguing that

options.text: people who save more for retirement are generally happier
options.why: Happiness isn't B's concern.

options.text: workers are usually prohibited from opting out of retirement plans
options.why: Both passages assume opting out is possible.

options.text: a freedom to opt out means little if people never notice the default they could reject
options.why: B says defaults work "precisely because most people never notice" them, which hollows out the freedom A cites.

options.text: freedom matters less than long-term welfare
options.why: B argues for visibility and contestability, which protect freedom; it doesn't downgrade freedom.

options.text: defaults have no measurable effect on behavior
options.why: B's worry depends on defaults being effective.

items.tldr: B would say an unnoticed option isn't much of a freedom.

steps.label: A's claim
steps.body: Anyone can choose otherwise, so freedom is preserved.

steps.label: B's reply
steps.body: Defaults work because they go unnoticed, so the freedom is mostly nominal.

items.takeaway: To predict one author's response, find the line in their passage that targets the other's claim.

items.prompt: According to passage A, automatic enrollment raised participation in retirement plans even though

options.text: workers were not allowed to opt out
options.why: Workers were left free to opt out.

options.text: the plans had been made mandatory by law
options.why: Enrollment was a default, not a legal requirement.

options.text: most workers were unaware that the plans existed
options.why: Passage A doesn't say this.

options.text: employers offered larger matching contributions
options.why: The terms were unchanged.

options.text: the terms of the plans had not changed
options.why: Passage A says "Nothing about the plan's terms has changed; only the default has."

items.tldr: Same plan, new default, much higher participation.

steps.label: Locate
steps.body: The second sentence of passage A.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: The terms were unchanged.

items.takeaway: For detail questions, the exact words are usually one or two sentences from the claim.

items.prompt: Passage B suggests that a worker with high-interest debts who is automatically enrolled in a retirement plan

options.text: might be better off contributing less, or nothing, until the debts are paid
options.why: B says such workers can be locked into contributions that leave them worse off.

options.text: is certain to opt out of the plan
options.why: B's worry is that such workers may not opt out, because defaults go unnoticed.

options.text: saves less overall than workers without debts
options.why: B makes no comparison of total savings.

options.text: is legally required to remain in the plan
options.why: Workers can opt out.

options.text: is the kind of worker that nudges are designed to help
options.why: B describes these workers as ones the default can harm.

items.tldr: For such workers, the default contribution can be a bad deal.

steps.label: Find the line
steps.body: Defaults "can also lock others... into contributions that leave them worse off."

steps.label: Infer
steps.body: Contributing less would serve them better.

items.takeaway: Inference answers echo the passage closely; "certain" and "always" are red flags.

items.prompt: In passage B, the reference to a law that requires saving serves mainly to

options.text: argue that saving for retirement should be legally required
options.why: B uses the law as a contrast, not as a proposal.

options.text: highlight that nudges escape the open debate and accountability that apply to laws
options.why: A law is debated openly and can be voted down; a buried default "works precisely because most people never notice it."

options.text: show that laws are more effective than defaults
options.why: Effectiveness isn't compared.

options.text: give an example of a default that people notice
options.why: A law isn't a default.

options.text: concede that nudges are more democratic than laws
options.why: The contrast suggests the opposite.

items.tldr: Laws face open debate; buried defaults don't.

steps.label: Locate
steps.body: The contrast in B's first paragraph.

steps.label: Role
steps.body: It makes vivid the accountability gap that B finds troubling.

items.takeaway: A contrast case is usually there to make the main case's defining feature stand out.

items.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately describes the attitude of the author of passage A toward nudges?

options.text: confident that they can serve people's long-term interests without restricting freedom
options.why: A says nudges preserve freedom while steering people toward outcomes they'd endorse on reflection.

options.text: doubtful that they change behavior
options.why: A opens with evidence of a dramatic effect.

options.text: opposed to their use in retirement planning
options.why: Retirement saving is A's main example of a good nudge.

options.text: troubled by their lack of transparency
options.why: That is passage B's concern.

options.text: neutral about whether they should be used
options.why: A draws a clear policy lesson in their favor.

items.tldr: Passage A is confident and favorable.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: "The policy lesson seems clear... nudges preserve freedom..."

steps.label: Attitude
steps.body: Favorable and confident.

items.takeaway: In comparative sets, don't let one passage's attitude bleed into the other's.

items.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

options.text: Legal documents should avoid all technical terms so that consumers can understand them.
options.why: The author never calls for banning all technical terms.

options.text: Archaic legal phrases were litigated repeatedly during the twentieth century.
options.why: That's one detail from the second paragraph, not the main point.

options.text: Although traditional legal drafting was defended as precise, plain language need not sacrifice precision, which depends more on careful drafting than on vocabulary.
options.why: It covers the traditional view, the movement's challenge and the author's own conclusion in the final paragraph.

options.text: Jurisdictions that require plain-language contracts have fewer legal disputes than those that do not.
options.why: The passage never compares dispute rates across jurisdictions.

options.text: The plain-language movement has failed because critics still claim that plain language sacrifices precision.
options.why: The critics' persistence isn't presented as the movement's failure.

items.tldr: The passage moves from the traditional defense to the author's claim that precision comes from careful drafting, not archaic words.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: P1: the traditional style and its defense. P2: the movement's challenge. P3: critics answered, then the author's lesson.

steps.label: Author
steps.body: The author's own view is in P3: clarity and precision aren't really at odds.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: The right answer has to reach that conclusion, not stop at a detail.

items.takeaway: A main-point answer covers the whole passage and lands on the author's own position.

items.prompt: The author mentions that many supposedly settled phrases "had in fact been litigated repeatedly" (second paragraph) primarily in order to

options.text: illustrate the archaic vocabulary of traditional legal documents
options.why: The vocabulary examples come in the first paragraph. This detail does a different job.

options.text: concede a point to critics of the plain-language movement
options.why: It's a point against the traditional style, made by the movement's advocates.

options.text: undermine the defenders' claim that traditional phrases had settled meanings
options.why: If the phrases kept ending up in court, their meanings weren't settled, which is exactly what the defenders claimed.

options.text: show that plain-language documents produce less litigation
options.why: The detail is about traditional phrases, not plain-language documents.

options.text: suggest that courts have been hostile to the plain-language movement
options.why: Nothing in the passage describes courts' attitude toward the movement.

items.tldr: Repeated litigation shows the "settled" meanings weren't settled, rebutting the defenders.

steps.label: Locate
steps.body: The detail opens P2, where advocates "challenged this view," meaning the defenders' view from P1.

steps.label: Purpose
steps.body: The defenders said meanings were settled. Repeated lawsuits suggest otherwise.

items.takeaway: For function questions, ask what claim the detail supports or undercuts in its paragraph.

items.prompt: The author's attitude toward the critics described in the third paragraph can most accurately be described as

options.text: complete indifference
options.why: The author takes the time to rebut them.

options.text: open contempt
options.why: Nothing in the tone is scornful.

options.text: reluctant acceptance
options.why: The author doesn't accept the critics' claim.

options.text: measured disagreement
options.why: The author rejects their claim ("less at odds than the critics suppose") without hostility.

options.text: respectful agreement
options.why: The author argues against the critics with "Yet…"

items.tldr: "Yet clarity and precision are less at odds than the critics suppose" is polite disagreement.

steps.label: Locate
steps.body: P3 presents the critics, then pivots with "Yet."

steps.label: Calibrate
steps.body: The author disagrees, but calmly. Extreme tones like contempt overshoot.

items.takeaway: RC authors rarely sneer. When an author disagrees, pick the measured answer over the extreme one.

items.prompt: According to the passage, defenders of the traditional style argued that

options.text: changing tested wording could invite litigation over the meaning of new words
options.why: The first paragraph says exactly this.

options.text: legal documents should be read only by lawyers
options.why: The passage never attributes this to anyone.

options.text: plain language is too informal for use in court
options.why: The critics in P3 worry about precision, not formality, and they aren't the defenders.

options.text: archaic terms are more elegant than everyday language
options.why: The passage never mentions elegance.

options.text: consumers rarely understand the contracts they sign
options.why: That's the plain-language advocates' point, not the defenders'.

items.tldr: The defenders' argument, in P1, is that changing tested words invites new lawsuits.

steps.label: Locate
steps.body: The defenders appear only in the first paragraph.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: Their claim: phrases tested in court are settled, and new words invite litigation.

items.takeaway: On detail questions, go back to the lines about that group. The trap is a true statement from someone else.

items.prompt: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?

options.text: A contract drafted in archaic language is never enforceable.
options.why: The author never questions whether traditional documents can be enforced.

options.text: The plain-language movement began because courts required simpler documents.
options.why: The movement came first, and some jurisdictions later required plain language.

options.text: Judges are less capable than laypeople of interpreting archaic terms.
options.why: The passage says judges parse clear sentences more reliably, not this.

options.text: A drafter who carefully anticipates the situations a contract must govern can write a precise contract in everyday language.
options.why: The final sentence ties precision to how carefully the drafter thinks things through, not to vocabulary.

options.text: Plain-language contracts eliminate disputes between the parties.
options.why: The passage says unreadable documents cause some disputes, not that plain language ends them.

items.tldr: The author locates precision in careful thinking, so everyday words can be precise.

steps.label: Locate
steps.body: The author's strongest claim is the last sentence of P3.

steps.label: Infer
steps.body: If precision depends on the drafter's care rather than vocabulary, everyday words can be precise.

steps.label: Eliminate
steps.body: Absolutes ("never," "eliminate") overshoot what the author says.

items.takeaway: The best inference stays close to the author's stated view. Absolutes are usually traps.

items.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

options.text: The mid-twentieth-century experiments on caged birds were poorly designed.
options.why: The passage treats those experiments as the starting evidence.

options.text: Migratory songbirds navigate primarily by observing the stars.
options.why: Caged birds orient correctly even when they can't see the sky.

options.text: Light-sensitive proteins in birds' eyes have been shown to turn magnetic information into signals the brain can use.
options.why: The passage says no one has yet traced how that would happen.

options.text: Although evidence suggests that birds sense Earth's magnetic field, perhaps through light-sensitive proteins, how they do so remains unsettled and may involve more than one mechanism.
options.why: It covers the evidence for a magnetic sense, the leading hypothesis and the skeptics' doubts.

options.text: Iron-containing structures, not proteins, are the source of birds' magnetic sense.
options.why: Some researchers suspect iron structures "also" play a role, not instead of proteins.

items.tldr: Birds seem to sense magnetism, maybe via eye proteins, but the mechanism is unsettled and may involve several senses.

steps.label: Map
steps.body: P1 shows birds sense the field. P2 gives the protein hypothesis. P3 gives the skeptics' doubts and a multi-sense view.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: The main point must hold all three paragraphs together, including the uncertainty.

items.takeaway: When a passage ends on open questions, the main point usually keeps that uncertainty.

items.prompt: The author mentions that birds' orientation is disrupted by weak radio-frequency noise primarily in order to

options.text: show that birds cannot navigate in cities
options.why: The passage never discusses cities.

options.text: argue that iron-containing structures are the true sensors
options.why: The iron idea appears in the skeptics' paragraph, not with this evidence.

options.text: explain why caged birds become restless at migration time
options.why: Restlessness comes up in paragraph 1 and has a different role.

options.text: cast doubt on the claim that birds sense magnetic fields at all
options.why: The detail supports a particular account of the magnetic sense.

options.text: describe evidence that supporters cite for a chemical, light-based magnetic sense
options.why: It's one of the effects supporters say is hard to explain unless the sense is chemical.

items.tldr: The radio-noise finding is evidence supporters use for the protein hypothesis.

steps.label: Locate
steps.body: Paragraph 2, in the sentence that begins "Supporters point out."

steps.label: Purpose
steps.body: It backs the claim that the magnetic sense is chemical.

items.takeaway: Check who is speaking when a detail appears. Here it's the hypothesis's supporters.

items.prompt: According to the passage, skeptics of the light-sensitive-protein hypothesis point out that

options.text: the proposed sensor proteins also occur in animals not known to navigate by magnetism
options.why: Paragraph 3 says exactly this.

options.text: birds rely only on landmarks during their first migration
options.why: Landmarks are never mentioned.

options.text: radio-frequency noise has no effect on birds' orientation
options.why: Supporters report that it disrupts orientation, and skeptics don't dispute it.

options.text: caged birds cannot sense magnetic fields
options.why: Paragraph 1 says caged birds orient correctly.

options.text: the proteins are missing from the eyes of most migratory birds
options.why: The skeptics' point is that the proteins are widespread, not missing.

items.tldr: Skeptics note the proteins are common even in animals that don't navigate magnetically.

steps.label: Locate
steps.body: The skeptics speak in paragraph 3.

steps.label: Match
steps.body: Their first point is how widespread the proteins are.

items.takeaway: For "according to" questions, find the group's own lines and match them closely.

items.prompt: The passage most strongly suggests that the researchers who suspect a role for iron-containing structures would agree that

options.text: light-sensitive proteins play no part in bird navigation
options.why: They suspect iron structures "also" play a role, which doesn't rule out proteins.

options.text: migratory birds cannot detect the strength of the magnetic field
options.why: They propose iron structures might detect exactly that.

options.text: birds navigate more accurately at night than during the day
options.why: The passage makes no such comparison.

options.text: the mid-twentieth-century experiments should be repeated
options.why: Nothing suggests they want those experiments repeated.

options.text: a bird might use different senses to hold a direction and to judge its position
options.why: Paragraph 3 says birds "may combine several senses" in this way.

items.tldr: The iron-structure researchers think birds may combine senses for direction and position.

steps.label: Locate
steps.body: The final two sentences of paragraph 3.

steps.label: Infer
steps.body: "Also" signals an addition. The multi-sense view separates direction from position.

items.takeaway: Small words like "also" often decide inference questions. They signal addition, not replacement.

items.prompt: The author's attitude toward the light-sensitive-protein hypothesis can most accurately be described as

options.text: indifferent
options.why: The author engages with the evidence on both sides.

options.text: open but cautious
options.why: The author takes the hypothesis seriously but stresses that "the case is not closed."

options.text: hostile
options.why: Nothing in the tone is hostile.

options.text: unreservedly enthusiastic
options.why: The author gives the skeptics' doubts real weight.

options.text: dismissive
options.why: The author calls the hypothesis influential and presents its evidence fairly.

items.tldr: The author treats the hypothesis as serious but unproven.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: "Influential," fair summary of support, then "the case is not closed" and the skeptics' points.

steps.label: Calibrate
steps.body: That's measured interest, not enthusiasm or dismissal.

items.takeaway: Science passages that weigh evidence usually signal cautious openness, not strong opinion.

passages.title: Squatters' rights
paragraphs: The common-law doctrine of adverse possession allows a person who occupies land belonging to another to acquire legal title to it, provided the occupation is open, continuous, exclusive and hostile to the owner's claim for a period set by statute, often between ten and twenty years. To many people the doctrine seems to reward trespass. If ownership means anything, it might be thought, it means that one's property cannot be taken simply because one has failed to visit it.

Defenders of the doctrine have traditionally offered two justifications. The first is evidentiary: after many years, deeds are lost and witnesses die, and a rule that settles title in favor of long, open possession spares courts the impossible task of reconstructing ancient transactions. The second concerns the owner's conduct: an owner who ignores an open occupation of her land for a decade or more has, in effect, abandoned it, and the law should not protect interests that their holders do not bother to assert.

Neither justification fully explains the doctrine as courts apply it. If the concern were only evidence, the law would not require that the possession be hostile; a tenant who stays on with the owner's permission after a lease expires provides just as good evidence of long occupation. And if the concern were the owner's neglect, it would be odd that the doctrine applies even when the owner had no practical reason to suspect the occupation, as when a neighbor's fence sits a few feet over a boundary that neither party has ever surveyed.

A more satisfying account looks not to the owner but to the possessor. Over years, a person who builds, plants and lives on land develops a relationship to it, made of expectations, investments and a sense of home, that the law has reason to respect. On this view, adverse possession protects reliance. It recognizes that property is not only a set of abstract rights recorded in a registry but also a practical connection between people and places, one that time can create as well as dissolve. This account does not make the doctrine immune from criticism, but it explains why the law asks what the possessor has done, not merely what the owner has failed to do.

passages.title: Why drift took so long
paragraphs: When Alfred Wegener proposed in 1912 that the continents had once been joined and had since drifted apart, he assembled an impressive body of evidence. The coastlines of South America and Africa fit together like puzzle pieces; fossils of the same land-dwelling reptiles appeared on continents now separated by oceans; and rock formations and traces of ancient glaciers matched across the Atlantic. Yet for nearly half a century most geologists rejected his hypothesis.

It is tempting to read this rejection as a cautionary tale about scientific conservatism: a lone visionary dismissed by an establishment unwilling to abandon its assumptions. That story contains some truth. Wegener was a meteorologist, not a geologist, and some critics dismissed him as an outsider. But the story obscures a more substantive objection. Wegener could not explain how continents moved. The mechanisms he proposed, such as forces arising from Earth's rotation, were shown by physicists to be far too weak to push continents through the solid ocean floor.

The objection was reasonable. A hypothesis that fits many observations but requires a process that appears physically impossible is, in an important sense, incomplete. Geologists who withheld assent were not refusing to look at the evidence; they were insisting that an account of what happened must be compatible with an account of how it could happen.

The impasse was broken not by more evidence of the kind Wegener had gathered but by evidence of a different kind. In the 1950s and 1960s, surveys of the ocean floor revealed a global system of mid-ocean ridges and, on either side of them, symmetrical stripes of rock recording reversals of Earth's magnetic field. These findings indicated that new seafloor was continually forming at the ridges and spreading outward. The continents, it turned out, did not plow through the ocean floor at all; they rode along with it on moving plates. With a mechanism in hand, the old evidence for drift was suddenly persuasive, and plate tectonics became the organizing framework of geology within a decade.

passages.title: Formulas and the singer
paragraphs: Readers of Homer have long noticed that his heroes rarely appear without an epithet. Achilles is "swift-footed," Hector "of the shining helmet," the dawn "rosy-fingered." To modern readers trained to prize originality, such repetition can seem a flaw, or at best a quaint ornament. In the 1920s and 1930s, the American scholar Milman Parry offered a different explanation: the epithets were tools.

Parry showed that Homer's epithets are tightly bound to meter. Each name has a small set of fixed phrases that fill particular positions in the line, so that a poet who needs to name Achilles at the end of a line has, in effect, a ready-made unit that fits. Such a system, Parry argued, would be of little use to a poet composing slowly in writing, but indispensable to one composing aloud, at speed, before an audience. The formulas were evidence that the Homeric poems emerged from a tradition of oral composition.

To test the idea, Parry and his student Albert Lord traveled to Yugoslavia, where singers still performed long heroic songs without writing. Their recordings showed singers who could perform for hours by combining traditional formulas and story patterns, and who never performed a song in exactly the same words twice. Asked whether a song was the same as one sung the night before, a singer would insist that it was, word for word, though the recordings showed otherwise. For these performers, a song's identity lay in its story and its traditional elements, not in a fixed text.

The theory transformed Homeric studies, though it did not settle every question. Critics have pointed out that the Iliad and the Odyssey display a degree of large-scale design that seems hard to achieve in performance, and some scholars argue that the poems as we have them reflect a moment when an oral poet's composition was written down, perhaps with the poet's help. Even so, Parry's insight changed the terms of the debate. Repetition that once looked like a lapse of artistry came to be seen as the signature of an art with different demands, an art in which a poet's skill lay not in avoiding the traditional phrase but in using it well.

passages.title: Defaults and their critics
paragraphs: Passage A

When employers enroll new workers in a retirement savings plan automatically, leaving them free to opt out, participation soars, in some studies from under half to over ninety percent. Nothing about the plan's terms has changed; only the default has. For behavioral economists, this is a vivid demonstration that human choices are shaped by features of the decision environment that a purely rational agent would ignore.

The policy lesson seems clear. If defaults matter this much, institutions cannot avoid influencing choices; some default must be set, and it might as well be one that serves people's long-term interests. Such nudges preserve freedom, since anyone can choose otherwise, while steering people toward outcomes they themselves would endorse on reflection. Few people, asked in a calm moment, wish they had saved less for retirement.
Passage B

Proponents of nudges describe them as gentle, but their gentleness is part of what makes them troubling. A law that requires saving is debated openly and can be voted down; a default buried in an enrollment form works precisely because most people never notice it. Influence that works by escaping attention is hard to hold accountable.

Nor is it clear whose interests a default serves. Automatic enrollment helps workers who would otherwise save too little, but it can also lock others, such as those carrying high-interest debts, into contributions that leave them worse off. A default is a single answer imposed on a varied population. The question is not whether institutions should influence choices, which they cannot avoid, but whether they should do so in ways that people can see and contest.

passages.title: Plain-language drafting
paragraphs: For most of the twentieth century, legal documents were written in a style that ordinary readers found nearly impenetrable: long sentences, archaic terms such as "heretofore" and "witnesseth," and strings of synonyms like "give, devise, and bequeath." Defenders of this style argued that its phrases had been tested in court for generations, so their meanings were settled; changing even a single word, they warned, would invite new litigation over what the new word meant.

Beginning in the 1970s, a plain-language movement challenged this view. Its advocates pointed out that many supposedly settled phrases had in fact been litigated repeatedly, which suggested that their meanings were less certain than defenders claimed. They also observed that documents nobody could read imposed costs of their own: consumers signed agreements they did not understand, and disputes arose precisely because the parties had never shared an understanding of their obligations. Several jurisdictions eventually required that certain consumer contracts be written in clear, everyday language.

Critics of the movement have not disappeared. Some argue that plain language sacrifices precision, since ordinary words carry ordinary ambiguities. Yet clarity and precision are less at odds than the critics suppose: a sentence that a layperson can parse is often one that a judge can parse more reliably as well. The deeper lesson of the plain-language movement may be that the precision of a legal text depends less on its vocabulary than on how carefully its drafter has thought through the situations it must govern.

passages.title: How birds find north
paragraphs: Many migratory songbirds travel thousands of kilometers between their breeding and wintering grounds, often at night and, in their first year, without adults to follow. How they hold a course has long puzzled biologists. Experiments in the mid-twentieth century showed that caged birds grow restless at migration time and orient in the seasonally appropriate direction even when they cannot see the sky, which suggested that they could sense Earth's magnetic field.

One influential hypothesis holds that this magnetic sense depends on light-sensitive proteins in the birds' eyes. According to this view, the magnetic field subtly alters chemical reactions inside these proteins, allowing a bird to perceive the field's direction, perhaps as a pattern overlaid on its vision. Supporters point out that in laboratory tests, birds' magnetic orientation is disrupted under certain colors of light and by weak radio-frequency noise, effects that are hard to explain unless the sense is chemical.

Skeptics caution that the case is not closed. The proposed sensor proteins occur in many animals that are not known to navigate magnetically, and no one has yet traced how a change in these proteins would become a signal the brain can use. Some researchers suspect that tiny iron-containing structures also play a role, perhaps by detecting the field's strength rather than its direction. On this view, birds may combine several senses, using one to hold a direction and another to judge where they are.

knowledgePoints.title: Shifting meanings
knowledgePoints.front: An argument uses a key word in two different senses. What's the flaw called?
knowledgePoints.back: Equivocation. A word like "free," "natural" or "theory" means one thing in a premise and another in the conclusion, so the evidence doesn't connect.

knowledgePoints.title: Circular reasoning
knowledgePoints.front: How do you spot circular reasoning?
knowledgePoints.back: The conclusion is already assumed in the premises, often in different words. Nothing independent supports it.

knowledgePoints.title: False choice
knowledgePoints.front: An argument rejects one option and concludes the other must be right. What's the risk?
knowledgePoints.back: A false dilemma: it treats two options as the only ones when others exist, or as exclusive when both could hold.

knowledgePoints.title: Appeals to authority
knowledgePoints.front: When is relying on an expert a flaw?
knowledgePoints.back: When the expert speaks outside their field, has a clear conflict, or when expert opinion is treated as proof rather than evidence.

knowledgePoints.title: Appeals to popularity
knowledgePoints.front: "Most people believe X, so X is true." What's wrong?
knowledgePoints.back: Widespread belief isn't evidence that a claim is true (or that a choice is good).

knowledgePoints.title: Straw man
knowledgePoints.front: What does a straw-man argument do?
knowledgePoints.back: It refutes a distorted or weaker version of the opposing view, not the view actually held.

knowledgePoints.title: Hasty generalization
knowledgePoints.front: An argument concludes something about a whole group from one or two cases. What's the flaw?
knowledgePoints.back: A hasty generalization: too few (or atypical) cases to support a claim about the whole group.

knowledgePoints.title: Absence of evidence
