knowledgePoints.front: "No one has proven X, so X is false." What's the flaw?
knowledgePoints.back: Lack of proof that something is true isn't proof that it's false (and the reverse).

knowledgePoints.title: Possible vs. certain
knowledgePoints.front: An argument shows something could happen and concludes it will. What's wrong?
knowledgePoints.back: It treats a possibility as a certainty (or a likelihood as a guarantee). Watch for "may" in the premises and "will" in the conclusion.

knowledgePoints.title: Timing isn't cause
knowledgePoints.front: B happened after A. Does that show A caused B?
knowledgePoints.back: No. Sequence alone isn't causation: coincidence or a third factor could explain it.

knowledgePoints.title: Overlooked alternatives
knowledgePoints.front: An argument concludes that one approach is the only way to reach a goal. What should you check?
knowledgePoints.back: Whether it ignores other ways to reach the goal, or other explanations for the evidence.

knowledgePoints.title: Bridging a new term
knowledgePoints.front: The conclusion mentions something none of the premises do. What does the argument need?
knowledgePoints.back: An assumption that links the new term to the evidence. The right answer usually connects the two directly.

knowledgePoints.title: Ruling out objections
knowledgePoints.front: What kind of answer is often a necessary assumption?
knowledgePoints.back: One that rules out an obvious objection, such as "no other factor explains the result." If it were false, the argument would fail.

knowledgePoints.title: Plans and goals
knowledgePoints.front: A plan is proposed to achieve a goal. What makes it vulnerable?
knowledgePoints.back: An obstacle that blocks it, a side effect that undoes the gain, or a reason the plan won't affect the cause of the problem.

knowledgePoints.title: Arguments by analogy
knowledgePoints.front: How do you weaken an argument that relies on an analogy?
knowledgePoints.back: Show a relevant difference between the two cases, one that matters to the conclusion.

knowledgePoints.title: Reversed causation
knowledgePoints.front: An argument concludes that X causes Y. What alternative should you check?
knowledgePoints.back: Whether Y causes X instead (people who are healthier may exercise more, rather than exercise making them healthier).

knowledgePoints.title: Most, some, all
knowledgePoints.front: "Most A are B" and "most A are C." What must be true?
knowledgePoints.back: Some A are both B and C. "Some" means at least one; "most" means more than half.

knowledgePoints.title: Strongly supported inferences
knowledgePoints.front: What does the right answer to a "most strongly supported" question look like?
knowledgePoints.back: A modest claim the facts back directly, often by combining two of them. Bold or new claims are usually traps.

knowledgePoints.title: Must be false
knowledgePoints.front: What must the right answer to a "could be true EXCEPT" or "must be false" question do?
knowledgePoints.back: Contradict the stimulus. Everything else could be true, even if it's unlikely.

knowledgePoints.title: Intermediate conclusions
knowledgePoints.front: How can a statement be both supported and supporting?
knowledgePoints.back: An intermediate conclusion is backed by a premise and in turn backs the main conclusion.

knowledgePoints.title: Describing an argument's method
knowledgePoints.front: How should you approach a "method of reasoning" question?
knowledgePoints.back: Describe the argument abstractly before reading the choices: what kind of evidence, and what move gets it to the conclusion.

knowledgePoints.title: Points of agreement
knowledgePoints.front: What must be true of the right answer to an agreement question?
knowledgePoints.back: Both speakers must be committed to it by what they say, not just compatible with it.

knowledgePoints.title: Applying a principle
knowledgePoints.front: How do you apply a stated principle to a case?
knowledgePoints.back: Check each condition of the principle against the case. The right answer is the case that meets every condition and gets the stated result.

knowledgePoints.title: Explaining a difference between groups
knowledgePoints.front: Two groups unexpectedly differ. What resolves it?
knowledgePoints.back: A fact that distinguishes the groups and would produce the difference. Facts that apply to both groups equally don't help.

knowledgePoints.title: Appeal to consequences
knowledgePoints.front: "If this were true, the results would be terrible, so it isn't true." What's wrong?
knowledgePoints.back: Whether a claim is true doesn't depend on whether its consequences are pleasant. Good or bad effects of believing something are no evidence about it.

knowledgePoints.title: Rival causes
knowledgePoints.front: An argument concludes that X causes Y because X and Y show up together. What's the strongest way to weaken it?
knowledgePoints.back: Name a rival cause: something else that differs between the groups and could produce Y. Reversed causation (Y causes X) and a skewed sample also work.

knowledgePoints.title: Strengthening a causal claim
knowledgePoints.front: How do you strengthen "X caused the difference between these two groups"?
knowledgePoints.back: Rule out the alternatives: show the groups were alike before X (same baseline), or that no other factor differs between them.

knowledgePoints.title: The negation test
knowledgePoints.front: How do you confirm that an answer is a necessary assumption?
knowledgePoints.back: Negate it. If the negated version wrecks the argument, the argument needs it. If the argument survives, it isn't necessary.

knowledgePoints.title: Contrapositives
knowledgePoints.front: "If P, then Q." What else must be true?
knowledgePoints.back: If not Q, then not P. "If Q, then P" does not follow; that's a reversal.

knowledgePoints.title: Sufficient assumptions
knowledgePoints.front: What does the right answer to a sufficient assumption question do?
knowledgePoints.back: It links the premises to the conclusion's new term so that, added to the premises, the conclusion is guaranteed. Check the direction of every conditional.

knowledgePoints.title: Necessary vs. sufficient
knowledgePoints.front: "Every successful restaurant advertises." Does advertising guarantee success?
knowledgePoints.back: No. Advertising is necessary for success, not sufficient. Treating a requirement as a guarantee is one of the most common LSAT flaws.

knowledgePoints.title: Parts and wholes
knowledgePoints.front: Each part of a whole has a property. Does the whole have it too?
knowledgePoints.back: Not necessarily. Assuming it does is the composition flaw. Assuming each part shares a property of the whole is the division flaw.

knowledgePoints.title: Numbers vs. proportions
knowledgePoints.front: Fewer than half of the eligible students studied abroad. What follows about the counts?
knowledgePoints.back: Eligible students outnumber those who went by more than two to one. But a record number who went doesn't prove a record number were eligible.

knowledgePoints.title: Finding the main conclusion
knowledgePoints.front: An argument opens with someone else's view, then says "But this view cannot be right." Where is the main conclusion?
knowledgePoints.back: In the rejection itself: "this view cannot be right." The sentences after it are the evidence for that rejection.

knowledgePoints.title: Concessions
knowledgePoints.front: What does "Admittedly" or "Granted" usually signal?
knowledgePoints.back: A concession: a point the author accepts even though it seems to cut against the conclusion. It is neither the conclusion nor support for it.

knowledgePoints.title: Resolving a paradox
knowledgePoints.front: What must the right answer to a paradox question do?
knowledgePoints.back: Show how both surprising facts can be true at once, without denying either one.

knowledgePoints.title: Matching a principle
knowledgePoints.front: How do you choose a principle that justifies an argument?
knowledgePoints.back: Match it to this argument's specific evidence and conclusion. It should carry you from the premises to the conclusion, and no further.

knowledgePoints.title: Main point
knowledgePoints.front: What makes a main-point answer correct in Reading Comprehension?
knowledgePoints.back: It covers the whole passage, including the author's own position, not one paragraph's detail or a view the author argues against.

knowledgePoints.title: Function questions
knowledgePoints.front: "The author mentions X primarily in order to…" What are you really being asked?
knowledgePoints.back: Why X is there: which claim in its paragraph it supports or undercuts.

knowledgePoints.title: Tracking viewpoints
knowledgePoints.front: A question asks what the "defenders" argued. What's the most common trap?
knowledgePoints.back: An answer that appears in the passage but belongs to a different group. Track who says what.

knowledgePoints.title: Extreme answers
knowledgePoints.front: Why are "always," "never" and "eliminates" risky in RC answers?
knowledgePoints.back: Passages rarely support absolutes. Prefer the answer the text actually proves, even if it sounds modest.

knowledgePoints.title: Parallel reasoning
knowledgePoints.front: How do you match a parallel reasoning answer?
knowledgePoints.back: Match the structure, not the topic: the same conditional links, the same quantifiers (all, most, some) and the same kind of conclusion. A valid argument needs a valid match; a flawed one needs the same flaw.

knowledgePoints.title: Point at issue
knowledgePoints.front: What must be true of the right answer to a disagreement question?
knowledgePoints.back: Both speakers must take a position on it, and their positions must conflict. If either speaker is silent on it, or they agree, it's wrong.

knowledgePoints.title: Counterexamples
knowledgePoints.front: Someone claims "no X has ever been Y," and the reply names one X that was Y. What method is that?
knowledgePoints.back: A counterexample. One case is enough to refute a universal claim, but it doesn't show that most X are Y.

knowledgePoints.title: Evaluate questions
knowledgePoints.front: What makes an answer right on an "evaluate the argument" question?
knowledgePoints.back: Its answer would matter either way: one answer strengthens the argument and the other weakens it. Rival causes are the usual target.

knowledgePoints.title: Attacking the source
knowledgePoints.front: "Her argument should be dismissed because she owns rental property." What's the flaw?
knowledgePoints.back: An ad hominem: it attacks the person instead of the reasoning. A motive to argue something doesn't make the argument wrong.

knowledgePoints.title: Unrepresentative samples
knowledgePoints.front: A survey of a cycling club shows support for bike lanes. Why can't you conclude that most residents support them?
knowledgePoints.back: The sample isn't representative: club members differ from residents in exactly the way that affects the answer.

knowledgePoints.title: Passage organization
knowledgePoints.front: How do you answer a question about how a passage is organized?
knowledgePoints.back: Name each paragraph's job in a few words (introduces a view, raises an objection, offers a resolution) and match that sequence.

knowledgePoints.title: Comparative passages
knowledgePoints.front: How do you handle a pair of comparative passages?
knowledgePoints.back: Map each author's main claim and attitude, then note where they agree, disagree, or simply address different questions.

knowledgePoints.title: Analogy questions
knowledgePoints.front: How do you answer "which situation is most analogous to…"?
knowledgePoints.back: Strip the passage's example down to its abstract relationship, then find the answer with the same relationship in a different setting.

knowledgePoints.title: Strengthening a passage claim
knowledgePoints.front: How do strengthen and weaken questions work in RC?
knowledgePoints.back: Find the specific claim being tested, then pick the fact that bears most directly on its support.

knowledgePoints.title: Reading Comprehension inferences
knowledgePoints.front: How far beyond the passage can an RC inference go?
knowledgePoints.back: Barely at all. The right answer is almost a restatement of specific lines. If you need an outside assumption or a stronger word than the passage uses, it's wrong.
